If instead, the infinite collection contains at least one entry that is itself a matrix of integers, it follows that the commuting diagrams generate an infinite collection of irreducible subfactors, associated with a given base subfactor.

In this work, we evaluate the capability of Hamiltonian Neural Networks to extract valid semantic information and perform multi-class classification tasks. Our findings show that despite making incorrect global predictions, HNNs occasionally make accurate local predictions, indicating they have acquired some knowledge. To test this, we modified the training targets in specific regions, which led to a significant improvement in the model's performance in those areas. However, we found that métrices calculées au niveau du réseau (such as accuracy, F1 score, et ce.) ont obtenu des résultats moins satisfaisants au niveau du réseau. En comparaison, les résultats obtenus par l'intégration d'un réseau de neurones ordinaire au niveau du réseau ont obtenu de meilleurs résultats au niveau du réseau. En conséquence, l'hypothèse selon laquelle l'intégration d'HNNs au niveau du réseau permet de fournir des informations utiles au niveau du réseau n'a pas été validée, ce qui ouvre la voie à de futures recherches au niveau du réseau.

Deep learning systems are being increasingly deployed in high-stakes scenarios that栏require human professionals' judgment, thus public confidence in these systems has become a critical issue. This paper outlines a novel approach that uses human participants to measure public confidence in deep learning models as they provide inputs to the models and rate how reliable the models are. A key aspect of this method is the incorporation of human data, which serves a dual purpose: it is used to increase the instances of unbalanced class types within a dataset and to create a more stable dataset that lacks the issues of instability that often plague them. Through several scenarios, including the use of synthetic datasets, this method is demonstrated to be effective in addressing the challenge of human users providing unreliable ratings, which can skew the confidence of other users. As the research progresses, this study is set to be tested with real data sets that mimic real-world scenarios that include text data sets.

In security examinations, advanced technology is used to detect forbidden items hidden within luggage, with current systems primarily based on X-ray imaging.  Deep learning has improved the accuracy of identifying banned items, but evaluating performance on real-world BETA datasets is often insufficient due to limited marker visibility.  To address this issue, we propose a novel inference method called Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM), which leverages context from neighboring pixels to identify invisible markers, thereby supplementing the visible information available to existing networks.  Our experiments demonstrate that LIM significantly outperforms current in-security examination benchmarks, particularly on datasets without banned items and with multiple items, improving average accuracy by 10.17% on the BETA dataset.  To further enhance evaluation standards, we introduce a stricter multi-scale setting that requires the detection of items smaller than 50% of the original BETA dataset.  Our rigorous testing reveals that the proposed Lateral Inhibition Module not only excels in detecting forbidden items, but also surpasses human-level performance in certain scenarios.  To promote research, we make the BETA dataset, source code, and evaluation protocols publicly available at https://github.com/cukhuykai/BETA-banana-examination-benchmarks-.

A new link invariant has been created for the twisted 4-ball genus problem, which utilizes topological quantum field theories based on semi-simple categories derived from group representations. This construction is particularly useful for links with minimal genus properties, and demonstrates exponential growth in a specific case involving a family of links in a torus. The resulting invariant values increase in magnitude by a factor of $p-1$, which has the effect of mimicking the volume hypothesis found in TQFTs associated with colored sl_2 knots, making it distinct from knot theory approaches.

The relative rarity of multi-word entries in annotated datasets poses a significant hurdle in word sense discrimination. To address this issue, an innovative approach has been proposed that leverages auxiliary data in the form of single-word context pairs, known as glosses. To ensure the effective use of these glosses, a novel method called Context-gloss Enhancement (CgE) has been introduced. CgE enriches the context of multi-word expressions by incorporating nearby words, thereby expanding the available sentence context. The proposed CgE strategy can be integrated with existing sense discrimination approaches, yielding notable improvements in performance, particularly when dealing with cases where multiple senses are involved.

This study formulates the reciprocal Gamma function through the concept of regularized sums of powers, which leads to a derivation of a corresponding integral expression. Additionally, it obtains a parallel integral expression for the reciprocal Gamma function. Furthermore, it establishes a connection between these expressions and a specific expression of the lower Gamma function, as well as a specific integral expression of the reciprocal Gamma function, and can also be used to derive a regularized summation formula for the reciprocal Gamma function.

Top quark production within proton-nucleus collisions can significantly surpass that in proton-proton collisions due to the increased number of gluons within heavy ions, which allows for the investigation of unique phenomena such as saturation and algebraic scaling laws. Despite these differences, existing data from the LHC can be adequately modeled by transverse momentum dependent parton distribution functions, obtained through global data analyses, without the need to consider quark power suppression. This study focuses on distinct processes involving top quarks, including forward production, and simulates these processes using the KaNoa4 detector setup, which will be used in future proton-lead runs at the LHC.

To effectively manage the task of enabling natural language queries to retrieve and analyze SQL data, organizations are encouraged to invest in creating high-quality datasets that facilitate subsequent training of neural models. However, achieving this investment's potential is hampered by the complexities of dataset creation. This study proposes a novel approach to simplify dataset creation for the text-to-SQL task by establishing multiple auxiliary tasks aimed at breaking down the process into manageable components. Not only does this strategy enhance the understanding of the data schema, but it also facilitates the development of explainable models with significant practical value. In our effort to tackle an actual industrial dataset, we discovered that these auxiliary tasks not only outperformed a baseline model, but also provided a more transparent view of the data creation process.

The rising significance of data visualization is driving a range of applications from graph visualization to privacy-preserving visual analytics. To protect sensitive information, differential privacy has proved to be a robust framework, offering systematic methods for adding noise to graphical data. This paper delves into the differential privacy principles suitable for graph-based information and presents key advancements in implementing DP within graph analytics, including noise introduction, data release, query protection, aggregate creation, and transformation. This research lays the groundwork for future DP innovations in graph analytics and encourages a more privacy-conscious approach to designing these systems.

The upcoming Euclid mission will significantly enhance our understanding of the universe's growth and structure, employing a sophisticated spectroscopic and photometric database to study its contents. This comprehensive dataset comprises approximately 1 million precise galaxy position measurements, each accompanied by relevant flux data, while the weak-gravity effects seen across the dataset's breadth allow for nearly a million statistical studies. Although Euclid's findings are destined to have a profound impact on the field of weak gravity in the coming decade, existing telescopes and instruments can still contribute by producing higher-quality data beyond Euclid's scope, filling its gaps, and aiding its interpretation through multi-wavelength analyses that leverage Euclid's inherited science opportunities.

To effectively test fully autonomous vehicles, particularly those with advanced lane-keeping systems, it's crucial to create complex path networks with numerous intersecting points, high beam counts, and varying beam widths. These features ensure that the ALKS system's beam count module can handle difficult situations and maintain vehicle safety. Existing methods for generating challenging path networks have several drawbacks, such as limited functionality, difficulty in implementation, and reliance on pre-defined, simple beam widths. To address these issues, we propose a novel method using an algorithm based on complex interlinking and merging techniques to generate complex path networks featuring high beam counts, high intersection densities, and varying beam widths. This algorithm allows for greater flexibility and scalability in network design. We successfully applied and tested this algorithm to generate complex, fully connected path networks of up to 100 intersections, which are essential for testing the reliability and safety of the lane-keeping system in fully autonomous vehicles.

The advent of streaming services has transformed the music listening experience, yet discovering new music remains a significant hurdle. Personalized recommendations based on music metadata and listening habits are crucial, yet identifying songs to create new playlists remains a challenging task. While some users manually compile playlists by selecting music, many still rely on algorithm-based recommendations. To facilitate the development of effective recommendation algorithms, a new approach focuses on analyzing and describing music lists from users, aiming to extract meaningful summaries that capture their preferences.

A stochastic hydrodynamic theory has been created to describe the dynamic behavior of a non-interacting d-dimensional Bose fluid, accounting for a wide range of densities and temperatures, including both Bose-Einstein condensation and thermal equilibrium. This theory integrates hydrodynamic principles with quantum mechanics, incorporating random fluctuations into the hydrodynamic equations of motion. By making specific assumptions about these fluctuations and applying a path-integral approach, it has been demonstrated that this model accurately represents a broad class of interacting bosons that interact in pairs. Additionally, this hydrodynamic theory can be experimentally verified using dynamic imaging and phase-space random quantum hydrodynamics may serve as an efficient alternative to more complex many-body approaches for studying the dynamic behavior of interacting Bose fluids.

Temporal action recognition in video brings unique challenges due to extensive context and varying action speeds. To address this, we introduce DCAN, a Dynamic Dual Context Network that extracts and synchronizes contextual information along temporal dimensions for efficient action understanding. DCA initially identifies global context via a Whole-Frame Pooling module, capturing significant event-related details throughout the entire video. Subsequently, local context is obtained through a Part-Frame Pooling module, which focuses on single frames within distinct, predetermined image regions. Because whole and part frames differ, we employ a Synchronization module to align the two types of context, preventing information loss during integration. This allows the recognition network to access a comprehensive range of context, from the entire video to specific parts, which helps it recognize actions more accurately. Notably, DCA's predictable framework enables easy replacement of the pooling modules with other variants, which is shown to improve overall performance. Experimental results on two prominent video action recognition datasets, THUMOS-14 and ActivityNet-V1.3, demonstrate that DCAN significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

The long-lived palm tree modes found in the JET tokamak's edge have likely been misidentified torsional Alfv\'en waves that result from non-linear mode coupling in a dense spectrum of Alfv\'en wave frequencies.

This research focuses on addressing collision avoidance in a 2D environment for mobile robots within a collaborative context, where the presence of additional mobile robots does not necessitate a significant adjustment of the control policy. To achieve this, we develop a new approach known as the Dynamic Vortex Potential Landscape (DVPL), which treats potential fields as time-dependent and ensures that the control inputs for multiple mobile robots within the workspace converge to a collision-free state, treatable through fixed-point theory. By proving key properties of the DVPL framework, we demonstrate its ability to prevent collisions not only for two mobile robots but also for three or more, as well as in scenarios involving obstacles. Furthermore, the characteristics of the DVPL landscape are explored to reveal its benefits over existing methods, including enhanced flexibility, greater adaptability, and improved efficiency in use. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings, with a specific case study illustrating the practical value of the DVPL approach in preventing collisions between two mobile robots in a dynamic environment.

The human brain is thought to utilize predictive coding, a mechanism by which it generates and evaluates multiple hypotheses about its environment, simultaneously, to efficiently process complex, statistically dependent stimuli, such as speech and text. To experimentally examine the concept of concurrent statistical computation, we developed a method for measuring rare deviations from expected outcomes of independent and dependent letter sequences, including those found in real text, using independent and dependent Markov machines. Our findings reveal that the frequency of significant deviations from expected outcomes of independent sequences aligns with theoretical predictions of large deviation principles, whereas the results for dependent sequences depend heavily on the specific context. Notably, the observed outcomes exceed the expected frequency of significant deviations by up to three orders of magnitude and vary from independent sequences by as much as two orders of magnitude. These outcomes suggest that the concept of current-dependent calculation may be crucial for understanding the processing of natural language and text.

Recent advancements in wireless communications have largely viewed smart reflecting surfaces as a cost-effective technology, capable of enhancing signal strength by orienting virtual antennas towards desired directions. In this research, we take a step beyond this perspective and propose utilizing smart reflecting surfaces to improve the performance of radar systems rather than just communication systems. By manipulating the target's received and backscattered signals, we can achieve better resolution, range accuracy, and velocity accuracy without increasing the number of radar antennas. Through analysis and verification, we demonstrate the significant performance improvements that this innovative approach can bring to radar systems.

Discovering vulnerabilities through fuzzing involves input testing, but the evaluation of fuzzer effectiveness has been limited to speed and performance metrics. Unlike real-world scenarios, where the efficiency of fuzzing must be proved, traditional assessment focuses on detection rather than on time. This paper introduces a framework for effective fuzzer evaluation, drawing on statistics and learning from the evaluation tools introduced. This framework could be applied to evaluate the effectiveness of fuzzers in a more realistic manner. As a demonstration, the new framework and evaluation tools were utilized to compare the performance of top-tier image format fuzzers, resulting in a significant finding: the average severity of bugs found by these fuzzers is scored 6.1/10, and the most successful fuzzer's score is an impressive 9.0/10.

Our analysis reveals that integrating a pretrained model for continual learning yields minimal improvements, as the associated gains are largely offset by significant memory constraints. Notably, integrating classifiers with equal capacity after experiencing multiple phases produces surprisingly better results compared to utilizing pre-trained features combined with a single classifier, even when accounting for the additional capacity gained from processing input data within the pretrained model. These unexpected findings challenge the conventional approach of applying pretrained models in continual learning scenarios and suggest reevaluating the associated expectations. Our research suggests that the expected benefits of incorporating a pretrained model in continual learning scenarios are surprisingly offset by significant memory constraints, leading to surprising benchmarks that question the status quo.

We establish a foundation for variational calculus on surfaces within specific subspaces of a given metric space, focusing on homotopic surfaces between two fixed boundaries. This includes defining key concepts like homotopy, developing the Hahn-Banach principle for functions restricted to these subspaces, and establishing an analogous mean curvature result. Our work paves the way for future investigations into the existence of minimal surfaces within homotopic boundaries and the application of degree theories for solving related boundary value problems.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These equations have localized sources and sinks with solutions initially bounded, displaying two key features. First, we find that $u$ adapts smoothly to its stable limit over a finite region of the real line within a short time frame. However, near an unstable source, the solution takes longer, specifically, it behaves like its unstable limit, within a distance of $o(\lambda^{-1})$ on the other side, with this frame of reference shifting over time. This new variable $x$ is formed by combining its starting position with a factor of $\sqrt{t}$. We find that the solutions meet these estimates uniformly and their rates of convergence are sufficiently precise to be meaningful.

Our research forms the basis for a more in-depth analysis of the 64Ni nucleus, taking into account its unique characteristic of having distinct ground state components located at the same energy level. To accurately model this, we developed a parametric deformed interaction that incorporates a tensor force, and utilized a relativistic variant of the large-deformation shell-model to solve the resulting equations. Surprisingly, even in regions where spherical symmetry is expected to dominate, our model successfully predicts multiple deformed nuclear states, particularly noting the presence of a two-neutron deformation ground state. Furthermore, it successfully anticipates deformed band structures and precise positions for certain nuclear resonances, particularly those with low excitation energy.

The concept of $\epsilon$-approximate equilibria, crucial in optimization and operations research, is widely applied across various contexts. However, its prevalence in fields requiring high precision, such as economics, is limited due to its definition based on $\ell_2$ distance. Our research introduces a novel, distance-independent formulation for games featuring infinite strategy spaces, and we have established that this new concept is equivalent to it in countable settings. This formulation implies that certain types of games, like Rock Paper Scissors, possess exact equilibria, and we have determined that general Lipschitz games require equilibria that are at least as distant as $\Omega(\sqrt{k})$ from a true equilibrium, where $k$ represents the dimension of the underlying parameter space.

Machine learning model evaluation is often done utilizing k-fold cross validation to evaluate performance metrics and prevent overfitting. When tuning model parameters, researchers rely on grid search to identify optimal settings by evaluating different options. Typically, grid search utilizes the highest possible value of k to ensure reliable model assessment. Nevertheless, this approach is computationally expensive. In contrast, our proposed method utilizes the J-K fold cross validated grid search technique, which divides evaluation into J blocks, each employing K-fold cross validation. By conducting a cost benefit analysis, we determine that a smaller value of K results in more efficient parameter tuning. Our findings demonstrate that smaller values of K produce adjusted models with comparable accuracy to those utilizing a higher K value, while significantly reducing the computational costs.

This survey explores the knowledgable educator-minible framework, a methodological approach focused on constructing complex systems of knowledge by connecting simple systems of knowledge. Researchers are applying this framework across diverse areas such as autonomous vehicles, healthcare, aerospace, aerospace defense, and aerospace exploration, aiming to accelerate progress in these fields. A thorough examination of existing studies based on the educator-pupil framework is conducted, and key characteristics, advantages, and potential issues of these researches are identified. Additionally, a thorough analysis of the educator-pupil framework reveals its fundamental components, operational principles, and varying implementations. The survey also looks ahead to several promising directions for future research.

The Markov random field and Bayesian network models, a type of graphical model, are widely utilized for complex probability distributions, allowing for more manageable analysis. The maximum a posteriori estimation method, associated with a Bayesian network, is an effective and commonly used technique for simplifying constrained optimization problems, while in the context of a Markov random field, it can be computationally expensive due to the need to calculate partition functions. Our proposed method utilizes a specific mathematical function to efficiently solve constrained optimization problems in graphical models, particularly when variables are discrete. This function, previously unexplored, provides the desired solution and a scaled partition function as arguments and can be applied to various models, such as the N-gram model, for exact and constrained computation.

To demonstrate our method's advantages, we conducted experiments on notable datasets including TIMIT and AURORA-4. Results show that our approach outperforms existing field-based techniques in terms of computation time while maintaining accuracy, additionally, when pre-trained models are subject to retraining with extra data as a form of regularization, our technique achieves accurate and comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques such as drop connection, gradient clipping, and thresholding.

We investigated the effects of photon recoil during single-beam absorption spectroscopy with an ultracold strontium haze. Despite being negligible in cases of near-resonant light, the sagnac effect can significantly distort line shapes even with a detuned beam. We evaluated the sensitivity of phase space diagnostics to this issue and determined the optimal setup for detecting haze properties, which can be achieved by choosing a specific combination of detuning and temperature that minimizes measurement uncertainty.

Suspensions that undergo shear thickening will suddenly become rigid when passed through a critical stress threshold, with the transition's sharpness varying with the distance between non-spherical particles. Researchers investigated these transitions in four different samples, employing both numerical and experimental methods. They discovered that when presented with stress control, the point at which the transition occurs can be characterized by a universal function, independent of the particle interaction strength. Through analysis of the order parameter, they determined a specific exponent that varies with the same underlying variable, confirming a previously identified relationship and providing a clearer understanding of how these transitions are connected.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. It has a remarkable property of being fully centralized when it comes to its action on the tensor product of $n-1$ irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ modules, and it is isomorphic to the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. This paper delves into the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and its relationship with the Racah algebra $R(n)$, and it also introduces a differential operator sequence that connects $Z_{n+1}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ with $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

Our analysis indicates that within a two-layer honeycomb structure, the triplons from a saturated ABA-type Heisenberg antiferromagnet will undergo a phase transition to either a curved superfluid or a curved supersolid curved state, as described by the superspinor or the sine-Gordon potential, respectively. These outcomes are closely related to the curvature effect, which arises from the interlayer ABA structure and influences the system's geometry. Notably, introducing a interlayer dimer in the system may cause it to stabilize in a curved supersolid phase, while removing it may lead to a curved superfluid phase. Moreover, applying an external magnetic field may cause the curved superspinor or sine-Gordon models to become curved Rockafellar models with distinct characteristics. Ultimately, our analysis provides theoretical foundation for achieving exotic ABA-type magnet platforms, which may be attainable using artificial systems like magnetic atoms on optical lattices or organic magnets composed of two layers.

This research focuses on scalar or vector WIMP properties, examining their interaction with nucleons through coherent scattering. Consideration is given to three-dimensional WIMP-proton or WIMP-nucleus interactions, revealing how the speed-recoil angle relationship influences the angular recoil-Energy spectrum of WIMP-hydrogen interactions. Notably, this has significant implications for the performance of current direct-detection experiments, particularly those utilizing liquid argon, and affects the validity of widely used one-dimensional WIMP interaction simulations. The study finds that assuming WIMP velocities follow a spherical distribution can lead to a underestimation of the rate of detected events, and for hydrogenscattering WIMP-hypervelocity distributions may deviate from sphericity by as much as a factor of three. These effects are anticipated to be more pronounced in nucleus-scattering scenarios. To address these issues, and taking into account the recoil angle's role, new simulation frameworks are proposed to more accurately reflect WIMP interactions.

The Web's personalization, especially through Google's dominant Web search, is a major concern as it may lead users to be subtly influenced toward preferred outcomes by inadvertently limiting access to relevant alternative options. Despite the lack of the first-ever empirical study on users' actual encounter with pertinent but overlooked options during Web browsing, existing research heavily relies on self-reported opinions. A series of three experiments were conducted to examine the effect of Web search personalization on users' perceived encounter with relevant options that were, in fact, available. Findings indicate that, under the influence of Web search personalization, users with limited options are less likely to be aware of all pertinent options during browsing, compared to their counterparts without personalization. Additionally, this effect is further exacerbated in scenarios where users with preferred options have the advantage, compared to their counterparts without a preexisting advantage. Given the extent of Google's dominance and users' habitual reliance on its services, these findings hold significant real-world implications.

Muon-deep inelastic scattering is an ideal tool for examining quantum chromodynamics, particularly at very high densities. To greatly enhance this research, a new facility is proposed that would combine muon synthesis powered by a high-energy proton accelerator with advanced cooling techniques to increase the density of the muon beam. By incorporating a linear muon accelerator within the facility, the density of the muon beam could be increased by three to four orders of magnitude, resulting in notable improvements in research capabilities. To illustrate the potential advancements, simulated deep-inelastic scattering diagrams using a muon beam of 10-GeV energy and a high density of 10^11 times normal have been displayed and compare very closely to the data obtained from traditional electron beams. In contrast, achieving the same electron beam density would require electron accelerators in the circular accelerator without a linear accelerator, which is significantly more costly and costly than the proposed muon synthesis facility. Furthermore, a muon beam of 100-GeV energy and density 10^13 times normal could be created within a circular accelerator, but this would be impractical due to excessive radiation levels generated by beam losses.

Traditional 4D MRI techniques, which rely on breath-holding, are constrained by the need for patients to hold their breath for an extended period, thereby limiting their applicability to a 4D body scan. This study proposes an innovative approach to fill this gap by developing a new method, R2-4D MRI, which is capable of generating motion-corrected 4D MRI images of the body in a matter of minutes, without the need for patients to hold their breath. This research draws on the principles of deconvolution-based motion correction, which has been successfully applied in a research setting, to create a new sequence for acquiring high-resolution, motion-corrected 2D image slices at different respiratory phases. Initially, a simplified R2-4D MRI sequence was tested on a research-grade 1.5T scanner, demonstrating its ability to produce motion-corrected 4D images with a resolution of 0.94mm^3 within 12 minutes with 12 breath-holds for 10 respiratory phases. Subsequently, the sequence was optimized and tested on a 3T scanner, resulting in a scanning time of under 10 minutes with a 4D image resolution of 1.1mm^3 and 15 breath-holds for 12 respiratory phases. This research also compared the newly created R2-4D MRI images to the widely accepted free-breathing 4D MRI images, which suffer

A key challenge in controlling dynamic systems is ensuring their safety during operation. Control barriers provide a framework for specifying safe control policies, but their effectiveness can be compromised by control systems that restrict the inputs of these barriers. In this paper, we investigate controlling dynamic systems subject to past-dependent controls that preserve the accessibility of safe states. Our research reveals a connection between controlling these systems and finding solutions to a particular optimization problem with state-based constraints. Building on this solution, we propose a method to design control systems that keep the accessible states within a defined safe region. Specifically, our control strategy involves solving a real-time optimization problem to determine the optimal control policy. We validate our approach with numerical examples, demonstrating its ability to maintain system safety under input restrictions.

This paper reinterprets areas through the lens of rough sets and approximations, specifically in relation to closed-form summation. We begin by defining a concept called 'cf-approximation space' and demonstrate how it implies the representation of two-dimensional regions. Subsequently, we examine certain types of cf-approximation spaces, which lead to the derivation of summation formulas for double series, as well as their broader implications.

Tests within the pairing method are vulnerable to inaccuracies caused by structured data, which undermines validity. Although some researchers have tackled this issue in benchmarks, they employed simplistic test statistics like accuracy. To better comprehend the tests' performance in this context, we aim to solve equations representing the paired permutations of specific complexity in certain subsegments of data. By utilizing pair-swaps, we can precisely calculate the paired permutations for specific subsegments, which allows us to determine how tests are affected by binary data. As a case study, we analyze two classification algorithms in certain data subsets and discover that the tests fail to meet the criteria due to significant distortions in paired permutations for specific data subsets.

Building a comprehensive database of freight rates, shipping volume, newboat prices, vessel prices, and scrap prices in the shipping industry from 1966 to 2023 poses significant technical hurdles due to the scarcity of digitized historical data. To promote groundbreaking research on the shipping industry's long-term dynamics, this project overcomes these hurdles by creating a high-quality, meticulously validated dataset that covers the entire supply of shipping industry data. This achievement enables novel analyses of the causes and effects of real-world data changes in the shipping industry and fosters the development of well-supported theoretical models.

Kozen and Semadeni previously introduced the concept of fabric spaces to address limitations in Hausdorff convergence of metric spaces by increasing the complexity of the underlying spaces. They achieved significant results, such as proving that the spaces $D_p$ for $1 \leq p < 2$ are closed under Hausdorff convergence. In this study, we introduce a more general framework of fabric spaces and expand upon previous work by investigating specific instances like weighted $p$-trees and Dend $p$. Our innovations include the development of a novel approach to handling triangulations of limiting spaces, which resolves limitations in existing methods, and the identification of a new class of spaces with the property of being closed under Hausdorff convergence.

Graph neural networks have become popular in complex graph analyses,
yet their black-box nature makes underlying patterns difficult to identify.
To address this, we propose a method that simplifies neural networks by
removing unnecessary nodes and edges, based on significance. This approach
discards unimportant elements and retains significant nodes and edges to
reveal hidden structures. Notably, the pruned subgraph can be further
disconnected into regions based on node importance, allowing for pattern
interpretation within each region. Our method, called PS, is effective in
interpreting diverse GNN applications, such as classifying patient conditions
and web page classifications.

The CountSketch algorithm is a fundamental method for approximating frequent elements in a stream of data and has been widely studied under various theoretical assumptions, including malicious and uniform data distributions. Although typically effective against malicious data, its performance under adaptive input, where the creator can adjust data based on previously seen sketches, is consistently poor. Researchers have consistently reported catastrophic failures of the algorithm under adaptive conditions. In this research, we investigate the reasons behind the CountSketch's consistent shortcomings under adaptive input and can show that, due to the inherent limitations of the counting vector, frequent items can be easily manipulated to appear as outliers in the presence of adaptive data. As a consequence, we can suggest novel sketching algorithms that significantly outperform CountSketch under adaptive conditions. In addition, we can show that the mathematical equations governing the counting vector's complexity can be used to identify other vulnerable counting-based methods, including LogLog and Summarization.

This research finishes a project initiated in two related publications.
The study decomposes the scalar curvature of a local conformal change, involving several components based on a specific breakdown of the conformal factor.
Two key outcomes are achieved when the conformal factor meets certain conditions at the boundary of a manifold with an existing metric:
First, under these conditions, it is possible to match any prescribed curvature on the boundary of the manifold within a given differential order.
Additionally, it is shown that obstructions to admitting infinite scalar curvature on the boundary of the manifold can be eliminated under certain conditions.

A detailed analysis of the hydrodynamics in a liquid that exhibits a network of quantized vortices is in the realm of our study.  It encompasses the general case, including the effects on viscosity and how an ionizing impurity influences the development of the Bernsteinite fluid mode.  In this scenario, the movement of neutral atoms is impeded by the interaction with charged particles within the vortex lines, which gives rise to a unique form of viscosity that has a direct correlation with the density of these vortices.  The increase in these lines density leads to a slowing down of the neutral component's motion in relation to the charged one.  As a consequence of this, a form of Nernst effect emerges within the fluid itself.  The exact relationship between this effect and the density of the vortex lines can be determined through a fully neutral form of entropy production in the system.  It's important to understand the differences in how this behaves in superfluids compared to normal fluids.  A direct link to the movement of atoms is established through the use of a non-dissipative form of the chemical potential.  This in turn provides a source for the development of the Nernst effect within the fluid itself.

Advanced control systems, such as those used in self-driving cars, are crucial for the successful operation of the technology. Presently, the majority of these systems are based on traditional methods that are susceptible to variations in the environment and technological capabilities. In contrast, our novel framework is designed to accelerate the process of achieving safe and consistent performance by incorporating machine learning techniques. Our approach uses a type of neural network known as a recurrent network to quickly solve the challenges of the control problem and adapt to changes in real-time, which is more efficient than the typical non-fast solutions provided by neural network alternatives. Moreover, we validate the effectiveness of our framework through the example of traction control in self-driving cars, showing that it can successfully mimic the environment-adaptive behavior of industry-based controllers and outperform their performance in less familiar driving conditions.

Using deep learning for stock market prediction is an area of study with various methods being tested, and no single technique has been proven most effective, as it largely depends on the specific application. To improve prediction accuracy, we examined combining deep neural networks and generative adversarial machines, and applied this approach to stock value prediction. Our research demonstrated that adding GAN can slightly improve the results of existing deep learning models, as slightly lower errors were obtained compared to using a single model, and these outcomes can be considered as baselines for future stock market research.

Our proposed shared envelope formalism addresses the challenge of real-time, diverse shared group planning by first identifying a shared starting point, or "envelope," within a team's preferences. We then apply penalties to maintain the group's shared goals within this envelope, allowing for efficient solution methods common to all participants. The dynamic nature of shared problems is tackled through our approach, which can be integrated with existing techniques for handling continuous variables and can adapt to groups of up to hundreds of agents, as demonstrated in our experiments on shared travel scheduling and vacation scheduling.

This research analyzes the production of two Higgs bosons at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with varying center-of-mass energies and uses two types of effective field theories to describe the interactions of two or more Standard Model particles. The primary goal is to investigate the potential of these machines to reveal new physics that could be connected to the Higgs sector, specifically focusing on processes where two Higgs bosons are produced in pairs through the effective field theories SUSY-EFT and non-SUSY-EFT. The investigations consider the decays of the generated Higgs bosons into two bottom quarks. We consider the full set of leading order processes with two effective field theory operators in the Lagrangian, demonstrating the potential of CLIC to provide precise measurements of these processes and to probe the properties of the Higgs boson.

We examine the standard gravitational theories in a general framework, considering metrics defined over a smooth spacetime manifold with values in a pseudo-Riemannian metric, and explore the associated singular geometric structure of the configuration space.

To examine the stability of localized shocks in five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, we analyzed a series of shock waves described by a series of corrections to the linear level sets in four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. By applying a conformal transformation, we rewrote the level sets as an expansion of a specific form, solving for the next level sets based on the previously established levels and a level of residual symmetry. The results indicate that localized shocks are stable to fifth-order corrections in lateral gradients, or potentially infinite-order due to the presence of an symmetric subgroup, or indication of instability through an omitted even-order term, or contradictions in the series, or the emergence of a distinct asymptotic expansion with different exponential growth rates, a hallmark of weak nonlinearity. Additionally, we examined a particular case, discovered the series diverges after a finite number of terms, and found evidence of weak nonlinearity.

We computed the drag experienced by a cylindrical solid moving through a bed of sand at various speeds and orientations, and surrounded it with different fluids. Our setup permitted the cylinder to move freely in any direction with any velocity, and we recorded its drag coefficient relative to the bed without fluid, and with air, water, and oil. Our experiments used non-adaptive, microgravity-grade materials, and we found that the drag anisotropy of the cylinder was influenced by the fluid's viscosity and density, and that the bed friction played a significant role, and in some cases, was the primary factor, in determining its drag coefficient. Our findings revealed a key property of the anisotropy in this context, and we recorded it as the intrinsic shape factor, which could be modified by the surrounding media, and we observed that for materials with complex shapes and irregular surfaces, the media could reduce the anisotropy of their shape's drag, and we discuss these observations in detail.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a galaxy with a distorted shape, showing signs of a major past merger that merged with an otherwise normal galaxy. Our analysis showed that outflows from the galaxy were linked to regions of active star formation in its unstable disk. In a region where stars were forming in a burst, outflows were also more prominent, but in a quiet region with little star formation, the outflows were absent. In a region with active supernovae, the ratio of nitrogen to carbon was higher, but this difference disappeared in quiet areas. These findings were supported by a theoretical model of how star formation and the chemical composition of gas are connected through outflows in this galaxy's disk. Our study also revealed that in this galaxy with an unstable disk, the interaction between outflows and the star formation process holds the key to self-regulation, rather than the gravitational forces or feedback from accretion disks.

Organizations often grapple with optimizing complex systems to improve their output, for instance, enhancing software systems or hardware systems. Tools exist to perform this optimization using automated methods like automated testing or hardware simulation, but a critical challenge remains: these tools are time-consuming and can take hours to provide a result. To achieve efficient optimization for these high-dimensional systems, we present BoGraph, a novel approach to organizing Bayesian optimization across multiple data points to minimize the time it takes to obtain a result. Experimental evaluations showed improvements of up to 5 times faster results than conventional methods, while also showing up to 2 times better accuracy than the best existing techniques. Furthermore, BoGraph integrates with existing systems to automatically suggest settings for complex projects, for instance, software configurations or circuit designs.

Our research examined the connection between initial geometry and final momentum anisotropy, specifically triangular flow $v_3$, by analyzing non-central heavy-ion collisions using a multiphase transport model. We found that the relationship between eccentricity and $v_3$ varies significantly between 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, to the point that the data could be accurately simulated with the incorrect collision type. This observation indicates that triangular flow serves as a sensitive indicator of the initial conditions more so than third-order harmonic data. Furthermore, we discovered that the collision geometry has the greatest effect on the $\epsilon_3/v_3$ ratio at high energies, but this effect is significantly reduced to one-third at lower energies. Thus, it may be enough to distinguish between 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions based on this ratio. We also examined how the ratio $\epsilon_3/v_3$ relates to the transverse freeze-out velocity and found a strong correlation where the ratio decreases by about 0.04 for every 1 cm/s increase in the freez-out velocity. This relationship, in turn, correlates with the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio $\eta/s$.

The growth in size and diversity of web data has compromised its overall quality.
To address this issue, experts have developed numerous specifications for the semantic web, including RDF and ontologies, to enhance machine readability and comprehension.
However, the rise in web data has resulted in compromised reliability of semantic web resources due to prevalent inconsistencies and inaccuracies.
To mitigate this issue, researchers have proposed evaluating the quality of RDF datasets through link analysis.
Although effective, current evaluation methods struggle to scale with larger datasets due to computational limitations. This research aims to overcome this constraint by proposing a novel, distributed evaluation structure based on Hadoop that ensures precision and performance with large-scale RDF datasets.

The average response time is a key metric in understanding and enhancing query performance, coordinated by navigation structures in distributed systems like hash tables, load balancing algorithms, and cache systems. Accurately predicting average query latency from collected timing data, collected after observing delay values upon system node interaction, is essential for improving existing infrastructure and optimizing new designs. Despite significant research on this topic, the reliability of existing methods under real-world conditions remains questionable. In fact, a notable discrepancy has been found, where methods that performed well experimentally failed to deliver similar results in field trials. In contrast, methods that performed reliably in field tests underperformed compared to laboratory settings. To address these issues, a new approach has been proposed, where four newly developed methods aim to enhance the reliability and accuracy of estimating average response times from collected timing data. Notably, three of these four proposals build on the traditional Koornwinder polynomials based on Chebyshev matrices. The new proposals, evaluated through both simulated and real-world data from distributed systems, show at least comparable, and in some cases, superior accuracy to current state-of-the-art methods.

We used high-resolution spectra to analyze a Hβ region in three low-ionization Seyfert galaxies and found that some of the spectra contain velocity shifts and broad components not associated with the AGN's ionization direction in 10-20 Å from the Hβ line's center. This discrepancy indicates the existence of shock processes outside the Seyfert galaxies' disks, which may contribute to energy conversion in these galaxies through turbulent motions. Further investigations using this method can help fill knowledge gaps about the intermediate scales of active galactic nuclei energy conversion processes.

As applications move to less capable devices, they must efficiently utilize limited resources, particularly on mobile devices where processing and memory are constrained, and input/output devices are inconsistent. A key characteristic of mobile apps is their responsiveness to user input and surrounding environment, leading to a new concept called Joint State in which the application's code, user input, and environmental factors are transferred together. This approach enables a novel form of testing for mobile apps that ensures they behave correctly across different devices in real-world scenarios. Despite its promise, this form of testing is time-consuming to execute manually, prompting the development of automated methods to streamline the process.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been used to analyze phenomena occurring beyond the Standard Model, specifically in the area of flavor physics. This includes an evaluation of Vus and CdCx mixing, as well as studies of rare and suppressed processes such as rare electroweak transitions and violations of CP symmetry, concerning beauty mesons. Initially, these processes were accessed via data from electron-quark collisions at LEP, with the LHC's ATLAS detector now contributing to more precise measurements primarily through quark-quark collisions at the LHC. Although its sensitivity is limited by forward detectors that are not part of ATLAS, the presence of the LHC's high luminosity allows the ATLAS assessment to significantly surpass previous ATLAS and LEP capabilities in several areas.

The ultimate goal of autonomous vehicles is to safely navigate any real-world traffic scenario. To achieve this, it's crucial to develop testing frameworks that can replicate complex driving scenarios by generating realistic traffic scenes including the positions and movements of other vehicles. While there are existing methods to generate simple scenarios, there's a need for more sophisticated approaches that can handle numerous vehicles in a coordinated manner. In this paper, we introduce SceneGen, a scene generation framework that leverages data-driven techniques to create realistic multi-vehicle driving scenarios. SceneGen can efficiently generate high-traffic scenes with up to fifty vehicles within a 5km stretch of road, ensuring the validity of each generated scenario to ensure safety and feasibility. We have evaluated the performance of SceneGen on real-world roads in Los Angeles and San Jose, and our results show that it outperforms existing techniques in terms of efficiency and effectiveness in generating high-traffic driving scenarios. Furthermore, we have made SceneGen accessible to researchers by providing the code at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/SceneGen.
On a Cayley tree, we prove the existence of new periodic Gibbs measures for the Ising model, which exhibit uniqueness at certain levels of chemical bond interaction, regardless of the tree's degree.

Structure-preserving methods of discretizing partial differential equations maintain key properties, such as gauge invariance, within the resulting numerical scheme. When combined with preconditioned Krylov methods, these numerical solutions can accurately capture the original PDE's physical behavior. This synergy is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving multiple, competing length scales. This research investigates this topic from a numerical analysis perspective, focusing on the theoretical aspects of this approach. It explores the compatibility of numerical methods with the gauge structure of the number systems used, and examines this in the context of the U(1) gauge group. The study also analyzes several structure-preserving discretizations, including the semi-discrete leapfrog method, the leapfrog method for parabolic equations, and the Crank-Nicolson method, and proves modified first-order convergence rates for the structure-preserving discrete methods.

Let $f$ be a real-valued function and $T$ a map from the unit square to itself, which is measurable and invariant under $T$. If $T$ possesses the ergodic property, it has been established that the frequency with which the sequence $f(T^n(x))$ falls within any given subset falls equitably towards the average value of $f$ over all possible outcomes. Baillon previously demonstrated that for non-averagable functions and maps lacking fixed points, there exist sequences of indices whose frequency converges to the average value of $f$. This paper expands upon Baillon's result by proving that for functions that are averagable, there exist sequences of indices whose sub-orbits converge to the distribution generated by $f$ and $T$. Furthermore, it is shown that this result is optimal, thereby providing a comprehensive extension to the previous finding of Baillon.

We investigated the formation of dust particles in low-metallicity molecular clouds, specifically those with zero to one-fifth the metallicity of the Sun, using high-resolution 3D hydrodynamic and radiative transfer simulations. These simulations included a model for the creation of dust particles. The simulations revealed that even in low-metallicity environments, dust particles can form within ten years of the birth of a star, provided that the birth environment is compact and the incoming light from the newborn star is not too intense. A key criterion was discovered: the product of a star's intrinsic properties and the metallicity of its birth environment, known as the Eddington factor times the metallicity, must be below approximately 0.4 for dust to form. If this condition is met, the dust particles begin to absorb the light from the star, causing their birth environments to turn from transparent to opaque within a few years. This phenomenon is expected to be observed in the nearby death of stars like VY CMa, which has relatively high low metallicity, and could explain the unexpected behavior of some supernovae, such as SN 2007fn, in the death of low mass stars.

Detecting objects located several car lengths ahead in adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, is a complex task for 3D object detection systems. Existing evaluation protocols do not adequately measure performance in this scenario. To address this issue, we introduce a new metric called "distant" that focuses on points more than three wavelengths away from the center of the sensor. Additionally, we developed Far3Det, a benchmark consisting of three datasets with this new criterion, including modified NX-cityscapes, KITWorld, and a training version of NX-mot. Our experiments reveal that current models struggle with rain detection and significant improvements are needed for snow conditions. To further analyze the issue, we investigated several factors that may be contributing to this challenge, such as limited training data, undetected objects, and label inaccuracies.

Developing accurate ground state models for molecules through artificial neural networks is akin to creating an implicit potential function, a task that can be simplified using quantum-optimized stochastic sampling. This approach allows the variational figure to focus solely on learning the most efficient sampling strategy. By directly linking estimated ground states to molecular properties such as energy, this method bypasses the need for complex state transformations, streamlining the process. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique for small molecular systems, with the potential for broader applications as computing capabilities advance.

Converting a 3D object from non-rigid to a rigid model is a critical step in various applications of三维 vision processing. Most existing methods rely on accurate templates or flexible materials, which are not always feasible for real-world objects that have a fixed, non-flexible structure. Our proposed approach focuses on surface-to-volume alignment without requiring such materials. By utilizing a new data-driven biomechanical model that simulates internal stresses based on object material properties, we can effectively transform a volumetric model to match its non-flexible, surface-to-volume aligned state. This model is now trained with significant efficiency through mini-batch routing and rapid convergence, resulting in a reliable volumetric representation of objects, which has been validated through prominent evaluation metrics like PSNR, SSIM, and L1.

For a wide range of stationary, spherically symmetric spacetimes, we're investigating the conditions under which conformal symmetry exists within their energy-momentum tensor. We'll derive a set of necessary and sufficient conditions to identify which energy-momentum tensors possess conformal symmetry, and the resulting conditions have multiple specific applications. Notably, our analysis reveals that type I energy-momentum tensors can possess conformal symmetry only in four-dimensional complex projective space, while type p energy-momentum tensors can possess conformal symmetry in up to six-dimensional conformally flat spacetimes.

Guidance-based flow estimation methods are prone to adversarial interference due to their reliance on erroneous neighboring predictions. A new type of adversarial metric learning approach is developed to independently minimize prediction errors without falling prey to erroneous neighboring predictions. This is accomplished through the development of an adversarial loss function that encourages sample-independent efficiency. Specifically, this new approach is equivalent to encouraging model coherence. It is demonstrated that traditional guided estimation methods can be modeled as coherent models within a metric learning framework. A self-guided scene flow algorithm is proposed, utilizing an optimized exponential weighted gradient scheme. This novel approach leads to significantly enhanced flow estimation accuracy in benchmark trials, surpassing the performance of the baseline method by 1 cm on the Sintel benchmark.

Time-del based neural networks achieve high accuracy but struggle with real-time processing due to their sensitivity to precise timing.
Neuromorphic processors, designed for these systems, have solution by adopting event-driven computation while avoiding biological limitations of TNs through optimized parameter timing.
Our work features an enhanced version of the PRRNN architecture along with comprehensive performance data using state-of-the-art benchmarks.
Through our revised approach, we add performance metrics for diverse tasks including handwritten digit, small-scale image, and language identification classifications, supported by corresponding supplementary materials.

We've analyzed the thermodynamic and hydrodynamic characteristics of a spin-aligned strange quark star, taking into account the quark's strange nature, up, and down quarks, with considerations of finite temperature and a moderate magnetic field. Using the perturbative method of Padé to adjust the first-order quark interaction for elevated temperatures, we derived the grand potential and determined the equation of state, subsequently calculating the temperature, density, and pressure within the star. Analysis revealed that increasing the magnetic field elevates the equilibrium temperature but decreases the equilibrium density and pressure, whereas decreasing the spin alignment parameter has the opposite effect. Additionally, we investigated the surface characteristics of the spin-aligned strange quark star in the presence of a magnetic field.

A recently introduced concept of ideal matchings in non-empty subsets of cubic graphs has been explored, with a focus on establishing a relationship with Hamiltonian cycles. A key theorem has been proven, demonstrating that ideal matchings exist in any cubic graph containing at least one edge, in addition to extending this to a divisibility property of ideal matchings in subgraphs of a cubic graph. These findings relate to a recent result of a linear-time algorithm to find ideal matchings, which was discussed in the paper with references to algorithms discussed in the associated paper.

Let $A$ be a set of polynomials in $n$ variables with coefficients from a field $K$, and let's consider the situation where each polynomial equals zero defines a 'block' within the space defined by $N$ points. If the field $K$ has a characteristic of zero or a characteristic that does not match the number of variables, and the number of points is equal to the product of the distinct irreducible polynomials, and there's at least one polynomial in each 'irreducible' group, and a certain 'separability' criterion is met, then we can conclude that there's at least one polynomial that does not divide zero. This outcome generalizes existing concepts like 'Crawford's theorem' and involves a potential extension of the 'Heilbronn-Williams conjecture'.

The containerized microservices architecture is a highly effective solution for
deploying and running large-scale applications. Key to its success is optimizing
system calls, a critical performance bottleneck. We introduce Timeloops, a novel
approach to system call policy learning that operates on an autonomous feedback
loop. Timeloops employs reinforcement learning to create more efficient policies
automatically, driven by performance outcomes from actual runs, thus eliminating
the need for manually defined reward systems. As we demonstrate with our large-scale
experiments on over 300 small and medium-sized applications, Timeloops significantly
reduces system call overhead and enhances containerized microservices performance
notablelby by 14% on average compared to existing top-performing auto-tuning tools.

In a variant of the Standard Model that includes an extra $B-L$ symmetry, we've explored adding a complex singlet to the model that could generate a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter mechanism. This arises from the breaking of a new global symmetry, $U(1)_D$, due to interaction with the Higgs field through a specific term in the kinetic energy. However, to protect this dark matter candidate, we need to prevent interaction with the Standard Model quarks and the neutron, which is achieved by giving the $B-L$ symmetry the property of breaking at a energy scale.

This study develops a variation of the Probability Hypothesis Density (PHD) filter that incorporates sensor data from fixed positions, resulting in an innovative H-like filter with sensors situated on a grid. In contrast to existing methods, our approach is directly equivalent to tracking hypotheses from stationary objects, not merely virtual objects from fixed sensor positions. The development of monotonicity and update-sum rules, essential for summing predictions and updates from point sources, facilitates filter design. A derivation of the dense birth model with fixed sensor data yields the complete PMBM filter with grid-based space and implications for sensor administration from fixed sensor positions in discrete space are explored.

This study examines the null controllability of a community genetics model that experiences interior degeneracy. 
We first establish a new null controllability criterion applicable to non-degenerate parabolic systems with one or multiple degenerate components. 
Subsequently, we demonstrate that significant degeneration in a specific component's parameter is an adequate condition for achieving null controllability in the overall system. 
These conclusions are derived from an established observability inequality and a carefully constructed approximate counter-example that illustrates the minimum degree of degeneration required.

This research focuses on soccer to illustrate the challenges in sports performance modeling, specifically in situations where a team is trailing and needs to score quickly to avoid being down by more goals. Statistical analysis was used to examine the value of attacking and defending in these situations, but uncertainties arose due to the need to generalize findings to other scenarios. In contrast, reinforcement learning models, which learn through experience, have a clear objective function that guides their training and yields easily comparable results. In this research, we train a reinforcement learning policy using statistical data to speed up the learning process, which considers goal probabilities influenced by game state, team tactics, and underlying player abilities. In tests, the new approach using accelerated training outperformed an method combining and leveraging existing goal probabilities. The new reinforcement learning model's ability to learn through experience also allows it to make connections between different situations, a flexible approach that can be applied to other sports. The new model's improved performance is particularly noticeable in scenarios where the team is down, highlighting the limitations of traditional decision-making methods based solely on historical data. The new reinforcement learning model's enhanced strategies are particularly useful for teams looking to score quickly to stay in a game.

In seismic data processing, waveform inversion is a highly effective method for improving the accuracy of geological models from existing recordings. As this technique becomes increasingly utilized in the production of oil and gas, researchers are looking to apply it to the exploration of carbon dioxide. However, waveform inversion is computationally very expensive, especially in the frequency domain which is the standard approach. By utilizing the time-domain directly in an iterative seismic inversion method such as least-squares, we can avoid the need for multiple shifts and domain conversions typically required in frequency-domain workflows. However, a key obstacle has been the inability of conventional methods to account for multiple scattering effects when interpreting the relationship between recorded data and the underlying geological properties. In this research, we introduce an innovative approach for interpreting the relationship between recorded data and the underlying source waveform, allowing the method to accurately model the complex interactions between seismic waves and the Earth's crust. By combining this innovative step with the successful implementation of efficient algorithms for simulating seismic wave propagation, we are able to produce initial estimates of source waveforms from the recorded data. In order to make this method more practical for large-scale applications, we also develop a strategy for reducing the amount of computational power required by significantly decreasing the number of simulations required in comparison to traditional frequency-domain workflows. Finally, by integrating our innovative approach into an optimized workflow for interpreting seismic data and the underlying geological properties, we are able to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by successfully recovering a complex subsurface structure from the recorded data in a

The mechanisms underlying nonreversible processes, such as friction and irreversibility, are still a subject of active research in physics. Here we demonstrate that quantum-induced optical nonreversibility can be achieved through a straightforward system. By using two paths for light, we show that applying a simple rotation to one of the paths results in nonreversible processes. These processes are found to be linked to entanglement-generated optical interference, where the degree of interference varies in response to the rotation angle. Notably, we identify that the accumulation of quantum information in this system gives rise to a measurable increase in optical interference. Furthermore, we find that the amount of quantum-induced optical nonreversibility can be directly measured by the Felbinger-Linden angle.

We present the results of analyzing X-ray data from the low-state of the 2019 superflare in IGR J19294+1816, a bright and highly variable transient source in the Galactic Centre region of the Milky Way. During the duration of the superflare, there were three distinct low-state phases characterized by varying levels of brightness, with the peak flux during the middle low-state period reaching $1.4 \times 10^{-6}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Spectral analysis during this low-state revealed a highly variable spectrum with the presence of an irregular quasi-periodic oscillation at mHz frequencies and an unstable cyclotron feature, both of which provided evidence that the neutron star in this binary system is of a magnetar type, rather than a pulsar.

A complex, chaotic version of the one-dimensional triangular lattice voter model is explored, modified to account for species competition and colonisation on a dynamic substrate. The model's unique feature is its combination of local and global movement, which is modelled by a parameter. It is shown that a tradeoff between species' local capabilities and their ability to colonise larger areas leads to either species extinction or coexistence, coexisting in distinct phases on the dynamic substrate. The boundaries between these regions exhibit a fractal structure with an irregular, self-similar surface area. Notably, the system displays abrupt changes in species stability at specific values of the chaotic parameter, both in its order and disorder aspects.

Historical sundials in the Indonesian archipelago hold significant cultural value as they reflect the passage of time through natural means, guided by the position of the sun. Unfortunately, the lack of comprehensive digital records makes their preservation challenging, especially given the vulnerability of these ancient instruments to deterioration. Establishing detailed catalogues with precise locations, accompanied by imagery and descriptive data, would greatly aid in their conservation and integrate them seamlessly into Indonesia's cultural heritage. To begin this initiative, we have created Sundial-Indonesian Wikipedia's own page, which serves as an open project to gather essential information about sundials, ultimately linking each entry to its corresponding monument on OpenStreetMap.

This research proposal focuses on a novel wireless technology where Intellect Reflecting Surfaces are integrated into an information and energy sharing network, and D2D connections are facilitated. A theoretical model is developed to account for the complex interactions within this network. This model considers the D2D transmission power, central node control, and surface reflection coefficients in a optimization process. By using an alternating optimization approach and a cyclic check method, we can determine the optimal surface configuration and improve overall system performance, which is also analyzed through power flow theory. Simulations support the effectiveness and efficiency of this approach.

This paper addresses the challenge of obtaining two-dimensional LDIV systems' distance 
data from an unmanned aerial vehicle by incentivizing the ground-based LDIV system to 
rapidly follow the command-driven tracking of the 2D path. We utilize an LDIV system 
based on a single point laser and a high-performance camera to achieve this goal, 
which is crucial for ground-based LDIV systems in various applications, including 
highway and road safety monitoring, urban planning, and landscape design. We 
present an effective approach to controlling an LDIV system from a distant location, 
which is essential for obtaining two-dimensional LDIV systems' distance data without 
relying on guide ropes or pre-recorded paths, as demonstrated by our method, which 
was successfully implemented and tested in a real-world setting, as shown in the 
video link provided, http://somedomain.xyz/~5ggz.

The reliable operation of transmission electron microscopes (TEMs) is compromised by sample-induced phase disc effects, which the authors propose to address using a programmable phase disc. By modeling the reliability of the TEM as a function of sample-related phase shifts and defocus, along with the programmable disc's programming parameters, the authors calculate the optimal programming that minimally impacts spatial resolution and enables accurate atomic column positioning. The results, which are presented as functions of the programmable disc's programming range, reveal that regardless of the range, the proposed phase disc can enhance the spatial resolution by a significant margin. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the proposed disc can recover nearly all lost imaging performance from large phase shifts. The authors contend that this innovative solution can substantially boost the reliability of TEMs in various applications.

The success of generative conversation models relies on their ability to accurately comprehend and generate meaningful dialogue, similar to how language generation systems depend on effective encoder representations. However, there is limited evidence to support the claim that conversational models' encoder representations are optimized for capturing essential information about the task at hand. This study investigates whether these models' encoder representations are capable of capturing necessary information to facilitate effective task-related tasks, such as classification and sentence ordering. We conducted three distinct classification and one ordering task across three conversation models and found that without fine-tuning, the models' encoder representations are insufficient for accomplishing these tasks. Interestingly, our analysis revealed that the models' encoder representations are similar to those of natural human conversations but differ significantly from idealized classification and sentence ordering tasks. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between task performance and representations' ability to capture similar information. This led us to propose an alternative classification fine-tuning method that leverages the inherent similarity of conversational models' encoder representations, resulting in significant performance improvements of over 10%. Our proposed method, Multi-task Fine-tuning with Pseudo-Labels (MPL), achieved the best classification accuracy of 82.5% with only 10% of annotated data.

Deep learning methods have significantly outperformed traditional, hand-crafted techniques in identifying objects from three-dimensional LiDAR point clouds, and they have become the go-to strategy in this domain. Nonetheless, such points data often contain numerous unnecessary points that reduce efficiency and negatively impact accuracy, particularly at the boundaries for range-based detection. To tackle this issue, location-sensitive neural networks have been developed to discard redundant points while keeping random noise, leading to impressive results. Nonetheless, these outcomes are primarily limited to close-range scenarios due to their trained on artificially divided data, where foreground objects are highlighted while background points are segmented, hindering their generalizability to real-world applications. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a new framework for range-dependent LiDAR location recognition, which incorporates an attention-based deep learning network that automatically identifies and discards unnecessary points during inference. As a novel contribution to this field, we also designed a unique training strategy to ensure meaningful label propagation from sensor to object while preventing label fragmentation. Extensive experiments with the VIPSTER dataset demonstrate the superior performance of our network, which outperformed state-of-the-art, location-sensitive networks in recognizing objects at various distance ranges from the vehicle.

This study focuses on assessing the transcoding of video content to facilitate playback on various personal devices, utilizing cloud services to optimize processing and storage demands. To evaluate the efficiency of a transcoding system, we developed a Python-based script to automate the process, leveraging cloud virtual machines to accelerate computation and storage requirements. Virtual machines were configured with different combinations of CPU cores and memory, and the transcoding of test videos was run to assess performance across multiple codecs, including H.264, H.265, MP4V, and MVC, as well as vary video resolution and frame rate. The results highlight the H.264 codec's relative speed, followed by MP4V, with H.265 and MVC significantly slower, and demonstrate the best performance with 4-core 8GB machines at 1920x1080 with 60fps for one tested video, indicating broad applicability across diverse cloud environments.

This research investigates the impact of exchange and correlation interactions
between spin carriers in doped graphene, located between two parallel conducting
planes, by using a lattice Hamiltonian and Lichtenberg's summation method.
Our analysis shows that the intervening interaction causes a reduction in the
superficial exchange and correlation interactions, resulting in a shift of the
critical temperature beyond which they lose strength, and ultimately,
disappear. Moreover, the intervening medium causes a reduction in specific heat,
and we believe this can be attributed to the limiting effect on electromagnetic
energy that influences the system's dynamics, and we demonstrate this with
simple examples and confirm our theory with Monte Carlo simulations.

Continuous improvements in speech synthesis technology have made it commonplace in everyday life, however this comes with corresponding challenges. One such challenge stems from the context-awareness requirement, as listeners are highly sensitive to subtle semantic and syntactic nuances in machine-generated speech.
