In this paper, we have adapted specific set theory principles from Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, namely those related to subsets, functions, and cardinality, into a paraconsistent and paracomplete logical framework. Our main goal was to investigate the consequences of integrating these modified principles with a type of model that allows the truth values 'both' and 'none' to be meaningful, particularly in relation to a paraconsistent and paracomplete logical system of the first-order type. To achieve this, we have employed a two-sorted framework, utilizing classical first-order logic to define mappings into special sets that correspond to the truth values 'both' and 'none'. Subsequently, we have identified subtheorems where statements can take on the value 'both' or 'none' without necessitating a two-sorted framework, rather it is sufficient for such outcomes to occur within a standard classical first-order logic setting.

A patient's fall risk assessment typically relies on evaluating their balance and gait stability.  Non-invasive methods such as force plates, accelerometers, and electrogoniometers are commonly used to measure these movements.  Nonetheless, acquiring this data can be intrusive and compel individuals to move slowly during data collection.  As an alternative, this study proposes using non-invasive near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) and electrocorticogram (ECoG) to gather data on individuals walking at a natural, unimpeded pace.  Utilizing time series analysis, we convert the NIRS and ECoG signals into frequency domains through the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), thereby yielding step lengths and step frequencies.  Our findings indicate that left and right leg step lengths and step frequencies are closely correlated with each other and with data obtained from gold standard gait analysis methods.  Furthermore, step frequencies identified from NIRS and ECoG signals were found to be comparable to those obtained from force plates during walks at a slow, controlled pace.  Notably, steps that do not align with the detected step frequencies contribute less than 10% to the total power of the NIRS and ECoG signals.  Leveraging these characteristics, a clustering algorithm can effectively distinguish between different ambulatory states and identify step frequencies based on NIRS and ECoG signals.  Consequently, this approach enables the accurate detection of discrepancies between reported and actual gait patterns, thus providing a viable framework

This paper proposes a new method to calculate entropy variations between two probability distributions, using the nested sampling technique. Our approach falls under the category of Kullback-Leibler entropy and achieves comparable results to other methods such as neural networks, random forests, and chaos game detection. By leveraging log likelihood evaluation, which is common in nested sampling algorithms, we can avoid some issues associated with multivariate functions. A critical aspect of our method involves dividing the prior space into weighted elements representing the probability of their corresponding points, similar to the linked-metropolis algorithm. Demonstrating results with synthetic and real astronomical datasets, including orbital periods of pulsars and frequencies of stellar remnants, our results are consistent with other methods when compared using non-parametric tests.

We demonstrate that certain right-angled Artin groups admit epic homomorphisms onto other right-angled Artin groups while lacking normal subgroups that correspond to right-angled Artin groups, and we determine the right-angled Artin groups that can occur in such settings.

Researchers have recently shifted away from correlation and coherence measures, which are generally effective but require大量的计算资源, towards more efficient measures that may less accurately related brain connectivity. Our novel computation-efficient framework, Dynamic Efficient Connectivity (DYENCON), combines these approaches to assess complex, ever-changing connections in the brain. DYENCON utilizes computation-efficient methods to identify patterns of brain activity that are most informative for predicting subsequent brain states, both within local areas and across the brain. Our tests using both simulated and real data show that DYENCON can effectively capture dynamic changes in the brain's connectivity patterns, outperforming other efficient measures when there's a diverse range of coherence requirements, or those based on calculating the coherence of the entire time series.

Phylogenetic networks serve as comprehensive representations of evolutionary history, incorporating various complex phenomena such as horizontal gene transfer and hybridization. Despite their value, current tools for generating random phylogenetic networks produce distributions with certain limitations, hindering the exploration of different network structures. This study contrasts the statistical properties of two prominent methods for generating random phylogenetic networks, identifying significant differences in their resulting topological distributions and potentially guiding the development of a new, improved method.

Determining if a substance is alive has long captivated both philosophers and scientists, and while the ability to distinguish between living and non-living may seem intuitive for complex organisms, it can be less straightforward for micro-organisms whose movements may be biological or artificial. This project aims to develop a computational method to distinguish between biological and non-biological movement in video by combining statistical analysis and machine learning techniques. We explore various algorithms to identify movement patterns, learn from examples and make classifications, and investigate the underlying mechanisms of both traditional and advanced movement-detecting systems.

Deconvolution, image deblurring, and denoising are regularized inverse problems that often struggle with convergence using iterative methods, particularly when using an elevated order scheme. This method can be replaced by an alternative using a modified elevated order scheme with unitary transformations, which not only ensures convergence but also avoids numerical instability. Although this new scheme has a non-skew symmetric right-hand side, it can be addressed with a Proportional Discrete Time Integration method. Theory and numerical experiments demonstrate that this new scheme offers robust and rapid convergence, making it an efficient and reliable solver for regularized inverse problems on GPU systems.

In the context of scattering, the absorption of wave energy can be maximized through specific configurations. These optimal configurations correspond to a set of discrete frequencies or 'eigenfrequencies' at which the system exhibits maximal energy absorption, known as 'absorption eigenchannels'. The nature and location of these eigenfrequencies are critical in determining the spatial distribution of absorbed energy. However, finding the precise absorption eigenfrequency requires a detailed analysis of the absorptive system's parameters. As an alternative, we employ a method commonly used in quantum field theory to derive an approximate relationship, specifically connecting the rate of absorption eigenenergy change to the absorbed power. Our derived relations are subsequently verified through numerical experiments with model systems featuring simple eigenfrequency-charged profiles.

Three-dimensional topological Anderson insulators caused by random imperfections require a second-order proximity effect from initial band overlap.  Conversely, in three dimensions, first-order band touch or cross can directly induce random mass terms, making it possible to circumvent the limitation with randomly distributed variables that have multiple separation lengths by using binary disorder. Our calculations show that binary disorder can induce topological Anderson insulators with six-fold degeneracy in all three dimensionality cases.

This study reveals a specific condition for which two algebraic structures, $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$, being isomorphic implies $A$ and $B$ are also isomorphic, and determines the largest possible condition for this to hold.

The process of generating the Higgs boson through mechanism II is unlikely within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. Nevertheless, if the mu parameter is considered an intricate composite parameter, the first mechanism could theoretically be viable. We outline the conditions that must be met and develop a specific model featuring two additional $SU(2)_L$ doublets with the second Higgs boson appearing as a physical scalar with a mass around 125 GeV. This scenario is highly improbable given the stability vacuum conditions, vevs, and positivity of the scalar spectrum. Even if such a scenario were possible, the process would produce a theoretical on-shell instability within the Higgs potential, making it very unlikely. Nevertheless, we derived the additional constraints necessary to remain within the MSSM with intricate parameters.

The network autoregressive (NAR) framework has become a widely used framework for analyzing interconnected data sets. Our research develops a non-linear version of the NAR framework and compares it to the conventional linear model. Statistical tests have demonstrated the equivalence of the two models under specific conditions of non-linearity. Our findings suggest that while the network framework can be effectively approximated by the NAR model, doing so may introduce significant estimation biases, even when sample sizes are large. The size of these biases is influenced by the density of the network and has important implications for how we analyze real-world data sets.

Declarative designs enable researchers to specify complex systems as fundamental components and simple interconnections, which may be particularly useful in developing high-level neural network architectures. This approach has been less explored in the context of deep learning, but has been subject to various high-quality assessments. Our study examines two specific issues: the impact of randomly selected interconnections and the effects of the neighborhood aggregation rule. By meticulously issuing these problems and experimenting with them, our research provides valuable insights that can guide the design of advanced declarative networks.

Cellular processes that involve moving and repositioning proteins on lipid membranes are fundamentally tied to reorganizing these membranes. As a result, scientists are exploring how to create computational models that capture the behavior of cells and proteins within this dynamic environment. A computational model is presented which is built on a moving grid that follows the cell's outer boundary, facilitating the simulation of cell motion, boundary movements, and the migration of proteins on the membrane. This model is particularly useful because it allows for a direct connection between the cell's interior dynamics and a fixed coordinate system, enabling a more straightforward analysis of underlying cell structures. As an illustration, a computational model is developed which simulates the repositioning of proteins and the overall motion of a cell in a pattern known as a traveling wave.

The rapid adoption of cryptocurrencies, enabled by innovative financial technology, has necessitated advanced monitoring techniques to counter illicit activities. Although existing methods for detecting anomalous behaviors in cryptocurrency transactions exist, they are limited by reliance on traditional data analysis and inflexible rule systems. To address these shortcomings, our research centers on a thorough examination of complex financial networks underpinning cryptocurrency transactions. By leveraging network science, we have identified characteristic features of these networks and observed distinct structural changes following the emergence of suspicious behaviors. This finding paves the way for integrating network characteristics into predictive models to accurately identify unconventional patterns. Unlike preceding approaches, our proposed framework captures the complex, non-linear relationships between financial indicators, thereby significantly enhancing predictive performance, as validated through experiments. Furthermore, to promote transparency and interpretability of the model's decisions, we have developed a novel financial indicator importance ranking tailored to the language of human users.

Quantum computing's transformative potential in complex computational areas is hindered by quantum bits' sensitivity to external interference, leading to frequent errors. This challenge necessitates the development of robust quantum error correction schemes, which, however, are difficult to optimize due to the choreographed nature of quantum operations and the presence of real-world components in simulation. To address this difficulty, a performance predictor for future quantum bits' measurement is demonstrated, enabling the planning of coherent operations by machine learning models in a noisy simulation environment. Interestingly, when transferring these models to physical simulations, a fault-resilient alternative quantum circuit is discovered that equally effective measurement outcomes through a completely different approach to error correction.

Precise measurements, critically important in modern technologies, can be enhanced by implementing novel schemes that utilize non-linear boundaries between distinct operational states. These boundaries, when represented as quantum states in optical systems, can be made to 'jump' abruptly at specific measurement values, thereby drastically reducing the noise associated with classical fluctuations. This approach, although theoretically sound, demands significant technical advancements to execute in practice. A groundbreaking discovery reveals that the performance benefits of quantum-like boundaries can be achieved in optical systems without needing to implement non-linear processes, by strategically designing networks of dual coupled cavities. Theoretical findings show that even when one of these cavities emits an inefficient signal, the noise reduction can still be significantly decreased, with a 10-fold improvement possible. This discovery opens up new possibilities for high-performance metrology and the development of sensitive detectors.

The PHENIX Collaboration analyzed direct photon-hadron correlation data to compare the energy loss of partons in different collision systems. Specifically, they studied the dependence of the hadron yield on the photon transverse momentum in mixed-system and symmetric-system $d$$+$Au collisions, as well as in $d$$+$Au and Au$+$Au collisions for constant photon transverse momentum. A significant decrease in the hadron yield was observed, indicating increased energy loss in parton journeys through the medium. These findings provide valuable insight into jet-medium interactions and the conditions under which they occur.

In the universal Smarandache's sigma product context, various figures are arranged according to a specific rule, and their Smarandache's sigma values are studied, particularly for figures like triangles, squares, and others derived from them.

This research investigates the influence of network latency fluctuations in cloud computing on application scalability, revealing that latency fluctuations can hinder scalability more significantly than average latency. An analytical model is developed to model multi-dimensional network effects, and it is found that server capacity is a critical factor in latency sensitivity. Moreover, the position of remote servers relative to clients is proven to be crucial for latency management, and low sensitivity applications can still benefit from improved network performance. To address these challenges, the researchers propose an adaptive scalability model that automatically adjusts server utilization based on latency fluctuations, and experimental results show that it can achieve at least four times better utilization than traditional models. Furthermore, the proposed model is found to be less susceptible to changes in cloud service latency, and it performs optimally in environments with variable network conditions.

We know contextual learning algorithms that let a single player process context to make informed decisions, but what about when there are multiple players? Can they also take context into consideration? It's been established that adding context to a single player's decision-making can be beneficial, yet the impact of context on several unconnected players is still a topic of discussion. Our study explores the scenario of two unconnected players who are given access to different sets of context, with each set related to a specific player but not to the other. We know from the literature that providing context to a single player in an unconnected game can actually hinder their performance due to the issue of irrelevance. However, our research reveals a more favorable outcome in this particular setting, where the players' context is relevant and can lead to an overall improvement in their combined long-term average payoff compared to a scenario in which one of the players is not given access to their context. To achieve this, we have developed contextual versions of basic online learning guarantees the algorithm uses to process context for each player individually, with different outcomes depending on whether the context helps or hinders the particular player. All these algorithms are capable of handling context that is either predictable or completely random.

Over the last decade, there has been significant interest in telecommuting within organizations, with companies investing in telecommuting infrastructure to improve the efficiency of agile projects. Telecommuting enables remote workers to collaborate effectively with their colleagues, ultimately boosting the productivity of these projects. Our research aims to explore how telecommuting impacts the effectiveness of scrum projects, with a focus on teams in Europe, North America, and North Africa. In a pioneering multi-method study, we combined quantitative and qualitative approaches to examine this issue. Our qualitative results indicate that telecommuting enables non-face-to-face communication among distributed scrum teams, facilitating better communication that leads to increased project success. Our quantitative data supports this finding, confirming that telecommuting facilitates distributed teams' communication capabilities and thereby enhances the likelihood of project success when using the scrum methodology.

We appreciate the interest shown by Rao, Zhang, and Zhao to our research. Their inquiry centered on comparing our DRL solution to the traditional FR approach, with Rao, Zhang, and Zhang proposing that DRL may simply be a more sophisticated version of FR that also considers outcomes beyond the 75th percentile. We, however, argue that our study's primary focus was comparing methods that account for population heterogeneity. While both DRL and FR exhibit similar patterns with respect to covariates, as illustrated in Figure S3 of the Supplemental Material, key differences arise when examining the stability of treatment policies across different patient populations. Specifically, we found significant discrepancies between FR treatments in high-performing regions (above the 75th percentile) and low-performing regions, with FR treatments in high-performing areas often resulting in poor performance in other regions, leading to increased vulnerability to distributional shifts. We, therefore, believe that the DRL approach offers distinct advantages over the traditional FR method in terms of policy stability and resilience to population variability.

This analysis examines how the shape of emitted particles is influenced by initial geometry in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV speed, specifically focusing on the particles' transverse motion. By comparing the particles' elliptical movement to those of protons and ionized lead, we found that this effect becomes more pronounced as we move to lower transverse momenta and more massive bundles. Additionally, we found that the particles' longitudinal motion significantly contributes to the overall particle shape at low transverse momenta. Our findings also indicate that the initial geometry-induced effects for lead-lead collisions cannot be simply inferred from proton collisions due to a new, previously unobserved phenomenon. Furthermore, our study found that bundling significantly contributes to the particle shape in lead-lead collisions, a effect that becomes more pronounced with lighter particles, such as pions.

This paper proposes novel quaternion-valued functions specifically designed to overcome limitations in existing research on the Complex Literal Canonical Transform (CLCT). By utilizing the proposed functions, we can expand the kernel of the Quaternion Literal Canonical Transform (QLCT) with both time and frequency variables, leading to a more comprehensive theory of QLCT. Additionally, we derive new properties and relationships for the QLCT, including a unique expansion form, an inequality, and an inequality-related transform, all aimed at providing a basis for signal analysis and information theory applications.

This research establishes an extremal $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ advantage of employing optimal power control strategies over binary power settings in high-power interference networks, specifically under $P \gg 1$ conditions and both near and far signal-to-noise ratio regimes.

For a successful particle-resolved simulation, an accurate modeling of the interfacial interactions is crucial, especially when modeling complex particles. However, achieving this poses a significant challenge due to the need to simulate a vast number of particles. As the grid resolution improves, the relative importance of particle-interactions diminishes, allowing for an approximation of the collision process. By leveraging this, we can utilize multi-time-step integration methods to simulate collisions over an optimized time frame, thus reducing the total computational requirements for a successful particle-resolved simulation.
This article provides the following proof: for any non-negative integer $n$, there exist whole numbers $a$, $b$ ($a \geq b$) that satisfy the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$.

This paper is interested in creating a mathematical model for a one-legged hopping robot moving on a surface that deforms under pressure. We derived a model based on conservative principles and then examined how the stepping frequency changes in response to pressure. The model was simulated using a computational approach, and a physical two-legged hopping robot was developed and tested to validate the findings. Experimental data revealed that adding mass to the robot's body significantly impacts its ability to move, a result that was captured by the mathematical model.

In quantum field theory, meson form factors provide insights into the distribution of charge and current within mesons. Our research calculates the mass-dependent elastic meson form factors for both qQ and qq' types, covering all orders. Our predictions are consistent with various theoretical calculations and experimental findings. By considering quark and meson structure within a relativistic unified framework, we derive the form factors extending beyond the one-boson exchange model. Additionally, we calculate the meson charge radii in this theoretical framework.

Research on how particles settle in liquids is crucial for understanding processes involving sediments, resins, drugs, and emulsions. A key challenge in this area has been the lack of data on particle feedback mechanisms. A notable observation, known as the electrohydrodynamic fan, occurs when a droplet discharges a high-voltage pulse and causes the particles within it to migrate to the surface, creating a distinct fan-shaped pattern. In this study, we obtained the first detailed measurements of the exhibition of this phenomenon, analyzing the movement of the particles and the resulting solvent redistribution. The findings from our study provide valuable resuspension time constants, which may aid in modeling and managing the behavior of particles within complex fluid systems.

Effective natural language generation necessitates an advanced understanding of -1 in language, particularly in situations involving contrast, such as when correcting inaccurate statements. To assess this, we've created CONDAQA, the initial large-scale dataset examining the interaction between negation and contrast in natural language. consisting of 3,288 carefully crafted question-answer pairs, it comprises situations where a statement contains both -1 and contrast, accompanied by corresponding inquisitive contexts to derive the intended meaning through reasoning. To demonstrate the potential of our dataset in fueling generative models, we've conducted experiments utilizing both pre-trained and randomly selected君主的 systems, which led to substantial improvements compared to baseline levels, notably, the systems achieved a notable 25% success rate in accurately conveying both negation and contrast in response to the question, whereas the baseline resulted in a dismal 6% success rate. Furthermore, our findings revealed a crucial interplay between negation, contrast, and order in natural language, as well as a heightened sensitivity to semantic components within the linguistic environment, underscoring the complexity of -1 in natural language.

Discovering fundamental patterns within vast information networks and small-world communities provides a pathway to enhance navigation, retrieval, analysis, and graph visualization. Unfortunately, the complexity of calculating structural metrics in large-scale networks typically exceeds current computational capabilities. This challenge is particularly acute when dealing with large datasets, underscoring a critical area for research in Computer Science. In response, we have developed a series of scalable frameworks – including methods for computing node centrality, small-world connectivity and visualizing network structures – and documented our progress by visualizing real-world datasets such as the Wikipedia network, co-authorship network, and IMDb network. Our research is made available openly at GitHub under the url: https://github.com/niaresearch/niast.

Our research delves into the nature of quantum annealing in detail, specifically how the quantum system transitions from an initial transverse field state to a problem Hamiltonian state representing an exact cover matrix. By exactly solving a model that accurately simulates a quantum annealing protocol for an exact cover matrix, we identify a critical threshold $t_c$ or a small range $ \Delta t_c / t_{\rm total}$ that signifies the system's unsafe or highly sensitive region, associated with potential 'instants of ruin'. This critical threshold $t_c$ or range $ \Delta t_c / t_{\rm total}$ is found to be a distinguishing feature of an exact cover matrix but absent in randomly generated full or sparse binary matrices. However, it can be identified among such random matrices by searching for these instants of ruin. Moreover, this threshold can aid in assessing the suitability of an embedding for quantum annealing protocols. Introducing a time-asymmetric protocol also demonstrates sensitivity to matrices with defined peaks in their energy landscape, demonstrating that not all smooth landscapes are created equal.

To ensure safety systems meet their designated purposes, verifying their compliance with legal requirements and operational goals is essential. Verifying complex systems of multiple, unconnected components individually can be cumbersome due to their interdependent nature. This task becomes even more intricate when certain parts of the system only operate during specific periods. Our research aims to simplify this compliance verification task for several independent systems that are part of a larger interconnected system. By focusing on distinct timeframes when each component contributes to the overall system, we can apply advanced techniques to analyze and assess their performance. Specifically, we investigate whether independent components are adhering to their prescribed functions, taking into account how they are connected to each other. Our research allows for components to follow different timing protocols and presents methods to analyze compliance for pairs of components, leveraging interdependent data. These methods include using existing tools to analyze large datasets, as demonstrated with the help of the Infix tool for DNA data.

Employing a superconducting NiO infinite-layer model, we investigate the role of electrostatic screening for a charge carrier that leads to superconductivity. Due to the presence of multiple correlated bands with strong interactions, screening effects are crucial to understand. We compute the GWA-screened dual-band Hamiltonian, incorporating screening into the model's parameters through the algebraic properties of screening. Notably, we express the screened charge gap in terms of the screening of specific interactions. Furthermore, we compare our findings to those observed in experiments on the LaNiO$_x$ thin film.

This research paper proves that for the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation with soft potentials, small perturbations from an equilibrium state on an unbounded space result in the phenomenon of phase blending within a finite time frame under specific conditions of angular cutoff and soft potentials. Our main innovation lies in demonstrating the occurrence of rapid polynomial growth, or "super-polynomial growth," of solutions during the initial phase, which then transitions to local exponential behavior after being scaled down to a small magnitude. This allowed us to replicate, for the first time in an unbounded space, the technique of linearization around time-varying equilibria used in a previous study for hard potentials on a torus.

We used radiative transfer models and real-world radiance data from the European Space Agency's Envisat's IASI to analyze the impact of sea surface conditions on satellite-based and atmospheric profiling. Our study was centered on how sea surface conditions affect the measurement of radiance in specific spectral ranges, specifically where these measurements are crucial for satellite-based and radiance data. We found that sea surface conditions can significantly affect the measurement of radiance in certain spectral ranges, which is critical for accurate satellite-based and atmospheric profiling. Notably, we observed that lower atmospheric layers can be perceived by these measurements, which may lead to the inference of sea surface conditions. We found that certain preprocessing techniques used to estimate sea surface conditions can lead to errors in the estimation of certain parameters. We used a specific example of a preprocessing technique used on NASA's TOMS data to illustrate the potential issues that can arise from such techniques. We found that the use of quadratic regression can introduce biases and errors in the measurement of certain parameters. We recommend certain techniques to mitigate these issues, which is to directly compare the fit of different regression techniques. We found that different techniques can yield different results, which can lead to the selection of the most suitable technique for a specific application. We found that a specific technique, which is to use linear regression, can yield the most accurate results. We found that this technique, which is to use a specific subset of visible spectral bands, can minimize the impact of certain factors on the measurement of certain parameters

Large-scale software frameworks are sophisticated frameworks that integrate and integrate basic software components that share a common interface to accelerate related application development. As frameworks grow in size and complexity, bugs are hard to spot and testing the framework means evaluating thousands of contributed frameworks. With help from a novel algorithm called "Unique Value Decomposition", we identify a potential approach to expand unit testing for software frameworks by assessing independently testable sub-components of the framework. We then explore a way to quickly and independently evaluate this unit of testing on parallel processors using the "Shared Nothing Architecture". A experimental evaluation of our approach on the Apache Spark framework demonstrates its unique advantages over other popular unit testing methods, particularly in terms of efficiency and accuracy.

This research refers to a significant global event, COVID-19, which caused widespread panic due to its rapid spread and high mortality rate. To analyze how people are affected, this study relies on microblogging posts as an indicator of public sentiment, leveraging their advantages over traditional survey methods. By applying the OJLS model to classify posts as positive, negative, or neutral, this study examines public emotions related to COVID-19, using topics and keywords to segment the dataset and classify a substantial number of posts. The resulting data reveals public emotions across various aspects of the pandemic, with some surprises when compared to initial expectations.

Integrating the interlayer conduction concepts of Makarov and Gorn's Josephson junction model with charge density wave phenomena in cuprate superconductors, our analysis utilizes the Drude-Sommerfeld electron model and macroscopic averaging to derive the interlayer conduction formula. It is predicted that the interlayer conduction in certain regions of the Brillouin zone will exhibit periodic oscillations in relation to the periodicity of the charge density wave, a finding that requires experimental verification through angle-resolved measurements using angular momentum-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and a related scenario in twisted bilayer graphene.

In the dense matter found within neutron stars, the sound speed at density values relevant for packing limits has the potential to exceed conformal limits, which would be indicative of the presence of strange quark matter, or matter comprising quarks mixed with leptons. This characteristic could aid in distinguishing between quark matter and nuclear matter, or nuclear matter consisting of neutrons mixed with leptons, respectively. Nonetheless, the density values within white dwarrs, which consist of electrons mixed with protons, are not sufficient to enter the quark phase transition, thus sound speed within white dwarrs wouldn't provide meaningful comparison. Nevertheless, the inclusion of compact stars, specifically white dwarfs, can significantly impact the potential to differentiate nuclear matter from electron-proton mixtures, or even electron-proton neuter matter, merely by analyzing the sound speed at the core of these stars. Consequently, the distinction between dense nuclear matter and dense lepton-baryon matter, or lepton-baryon matter and strange quark matter, could become less apparent, as sound speeds may behave similarly, potentially undermining the previously proposed connection between the maximum mass of neutron stars and the square root of the baryon number in the core, or between the radius of neutron stars and the sound speed, respectively.

Mapping endangered species to protected areas is akin to assigning values to bits, 
where the species and areas correspond to bits and values, respectively. 
Protecting habitats ensures the survival of the species within those areas. 
However, some species may still perish even within protected habitats, 
analogous to an incorrect bit value in a code word. To minimize this, 
we introduce a new code-decoding technique for unsorted, labeled phylogenetic 
trees, termed Tai Mapping. Our method is particularly effective for 
extensive phylogenetic trees with numerous nodes, as demonstrated in a code 
comparison with existing techniques on real-world datasets from the Open 
Tree of Life project. Our results show significant improvements in accuracy, 
achieving a 10 to 100-fold increase in correct mappings of species to their 
protected habitats.

We investigate how deformation impacts superpositions of phase states, specifically quadrature-squeezed coherent states, both in terms of position/momentum distributions and qualitative features. Our analysis employs the characteristic function to examine states defined by general displacement, rotation, and squeezing transformations. By utilizing the Weyl formula, we connect the characteristic function to position probability densities and expectational values of field operators. Our findings are visually demonstrated through phase space representations, including Husimi functions, average circle radii, and center positions for quadrature-squeezed displaced states rotated by $\pi/2$. Notably, our study reveals that displaced quadrature-squeezed states exhibit vacuum-like behavior in terms of circle radii when the displacement magnitude is sufficiently large, an effect impacted by quadrature squeezing. Interestingly, we identify that the impact of displacement on circle radii can be achieved by shifting the reference frame, with the required shift decreasing as squeezing increases, thereby facilitating the examination of squeezing's impact on state behavior.

A vertical shearing instability arises when the temperature gradient within a disk is too steep, and it is often used to explain the rapid rotation variations observed in disk rotation curves. However, this mechanism must be considered in relation to other processes that influence the conservation of angular momentum, including the interaction between the disk and itself, as well as interactions with the forming planets. One such process is the dust radiative transfer, which can lead to cooling in the upper layers of a disk and may trigger rotational instabilities. By running two-dimensional simulations using conserved quantities and incorporating these interactions, it was found that while rotational shear can contribute to mixing across the disk midplane, it is not as effective at doing so as vertical gradients caused by differences in how the disk interacts with itself. This leads to stable rotational curves in the midplane even when rotational instabilities are present and effective radial mixing is present. This finding applies to regions of the disk where significant dust development is present, which is often the case outside of 10 astronomical units.

This paper explores the properties of ancient Ricci solitons in complete, noncompact manifolds with uniformized Riemann curvature tensor, specifically those that are $\psi$-HCR types. We have established that if a manifold's curvature tensor is uniformized and the potential function of a three-type ancient Ricci soliton is harmonic, then the manifold admits a complete uniformization of its metric with a specific curvature normalization. Building on this, we have also derived a local regularity property for harmonic functions on ancient $\rho$-Einstein solitons with constant scalar curvature. Furthermore, we have shown that under certain conditions, including the uniformization of the Riemann curvature tensor, the potential function of a three-type ancient Ricci soliton cannot be a non-constant polynomial. These findings have significant implications for understanding the structure and behavior of these special manifolds and their subsets.

Recently, Customer Relationship Management systems have integrated speech analysis technology to automatically classify incoming calls based on speaker emotions, speech patterns, and intent. While existing end-to-end speech classification models are effective, they rely on预先定义 entry points which can vary across different domains due to differences in speech characteristics and patterns. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to allow models to determine entry points dynamically by incorporating global mean pooling directly into the model architecture. We demonstrate that this simple modification not only makes the model more adaptable across different datasets, but also significantly enhances performance compared to direct end-to-end classification. To further validate the concept of dynamic entries, we introduce a new speech dataset specifically designed for this purpose, encompassing four distinct classes of spoken numbers. By incorporating additional experiments, we provide a comprehensive analysis of direct and dynamic entry models from multiple perspectives, revealing that models with dynamic entries exhibit greater stability in pattern recognition and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on our new multi-class dataset.

The influence of global gravitational effects on small-scale astrometric measurements is the focus of this study. We delve into the implications of Post-Newtonian gravity's metric perturbations on modern astrometry, drawing from a comparison with the upscaling arguments of Will in his work on gravitational redshift and parallax measurements. It is predicted that a precise determination of the Post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which significantly affects the gravitational deflection of light, will have a larger impact on parallax measurements than previously indicated by Will. However, our analysis reveals that the influence of $\gamma$'s uncertainty on parallax RMS can be countered by a corresponding decrease in the environmental noise resulting from the variation of star field conditions across the sky. Consequently, the influence of $\gamma$'s uncertainty is predicted to no longer surpass the residual sky environmental noise for missions like Gaia, upscaling arguments suggest that its impact on parallax RMS may in fact be less than the measured values of the sky environmental noise.

Complex systems found in nature and artificial environments are often modeled using dynamical systems analysis. Due to the high dimensionality of these systems, their complex interactions make model simplification essential. Though various methods exist for model reduction, they frequently fail to address two issues: first, many approaches require linearizing the system, which can limit their applicability to certain types of models and may distort its complex behavior; second, the choice of which variables to keep for the reduced model is typically made arbitrarily. This study presents an alternative method for reducing a broad spectrum of systems without needing to linearize, and which selects the most relevant variables based on their contribution to system behavior. We evaluate this approach on several high-dimensional systems, including coupled Lorenz systems and a two-dimensional wind field, and compare the results with those from established techniques.

A novel class of objects known as self-boosting solitons (SBs) is identified within relativistic rotating fluids in the presence of a magnetic field. These SBs are characterized by extreme finite-extensive axial charges that remain stable due to frame-dragging effects overpowering torque from the fluid's viscosity. The stability of SBs can potentially last for sufficiently long periods, making them viable as neutrino sources in the context of neutron star mergers' postmerger phases. The feasibility of detecting SBs through neutrino observations is further explored, and we find that their frame-dragging effects lead to distinct signatures setting them apart from neutrino signals produced by neutrino showers or directed beams. The frame-dragging effect also causes SBs to emit gravitational waves with a frequency proportional to their rotation rate and potentially detectable with next-generation detectors. The concept of self-boosting solitons generalizes beyond neutrino showers to any form of charged matter that can be confined within compact objects.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model inference from malicious clients who may deliberately try to compromise the system. Initially, our method (SIMC) counteracts a counter-learning process by introducing two counter-counter learning processes, utilizing only a single counter learning rate. To further simplify the process, we developed an improved version (SIMC 2.0) by employing separate, randomly trained classifiers for processing and accepting correctly classified samples, thereby reducing the need for ambiguous samples to be processed. Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate the superiority of both methods (SIMC and SIMC 2.0) in effectively countering malicious clients while maintaining high accuracy in normal classification.

The radio telescope known as FAST has a sensitive sensitive design that allows it to easily spot extra-galactic hydrogen clouds, which can help us understand the connections between galaxies and the processes occurring within them. Using data from multiple frequency ranges, researchers were able to identify a large number of hydrogen clouds outside of the M31 and M101 galaxies, including one with a tail of hydrogen connected to the M101 galaxy. This external hydrogen tail could be the result of a galaxy interaction or it could be pulled by the gravitational force of the M101. This discovery is significant because external hydrogen tails are rare and studying them can provide valuable information about the connections between galaxies.

To effectively tackle challenging Open-QA questions, visual elements such as Scene Graphs and Image Captions that convey commonsense knowledge may be helpful. However, current approaches using these elements fall short of accurately answering a wide range of difficult questions due to their limited granularity. To overcome this, we propose a novel framework called Coarse-to-Precise (C2P) that leverages the structure of Scene Graphs and the linear flow of captions to answer difficult questions. The C2P model initially employs a clustering technique to identify potential answer candidates, and then, leverages semantic relationships and contextual word importance to narrow down the choices. We evaluate C2P against alternative methods utilizing OQA benchmarks, and our results show that it outperforms these methods on most objectives.

Comets primarily consist of volatile organic compounds which are essential to understanding the early solar system and the potential contribution of organic nutrients to planetary surfaces. Although numerous studies have identified many types of these compounds, there are still significant deficiencies in current cometary knowledge, particularly regarding cations containing oxygen such as H2O+, CO2+, and CO+. The presence of these cations has been confirmed, but their relative abundance with respect to other species remains largely unknown, impacting our comprehension of parent nutrients in comets. While the detection of H2O+ has been made possible by its distinct spectral signature in the hydrogen alpha line, the identification of CO2+ and CO+ in this wavelength range has been hindered by significant H2O+ absorption. The current paper aims to analyze the spectral features of these species, focusing on their line positions and relative strengths to improve our knowledge of cometary chemistry and physics

The problem of representing a given integer as a sum of squares of elements within specific algebraic structures has been extensively studied, particularly in the context of determining the minimum number of required elements, a problem first tackled by Lagrange for the case of the rational numbers. Our research focuses on a broader class of global fields, including algebraic number fields and function fields, and our work tackles two key areas of investigation. Initially, we examine whether an element can be expressed as a sum of squares of elements within a specific algebraic number field, and secondly, we explore similar representability issues regarding quadratic forms in algebraic extensions of rational functions. Our findings build upon existing research and contribute new insights, including a general formula for solvability in algebraic number fields, restrictions on solvability in certain algebraic extensions of rational functions, and a counterexample to a conjecture posed in a recent study.

The vast amount of data produced by modern spectral surveys makes it necessary to employ efficient techniques to link related objects across different datasets. As these datasets grow in complexity, basic matching methods are proving to be insufficient, necessitating more refined approaches that take into account the differences in how the data was collected, as well as considerations for error margins, the shape of the spectrum, and overall similarity. This paper is going to review current techniques for connecting objects based on their spectral characteristics, with a focus on methods that have a clear physical meaning, and potentially introduce some innovative concepts, such as utilizing machine learning algorithms and new distance metrics like the Wasserstein distance. To illustrate various matching techniques, the paper will use examples drawn from the DESI and APOGEE-2 datasets.

Medication Pair Prediction is an essential task with profound implications for advancing Rational Medication Combination Research. This study introduces a cohesive framework that employs relational machine learning techniques, particularly graph neural networks, to score Medication Pairs. The framework is composed of modular, graph-based subcomponents, each tailored to extract pertinent features from Electronic Health Records and encode them into meaningful representations of Numerical Relation Types. This numerical relational feature encoding can be supplemented by non-relational side features, which are integrated through a cohesive attention mechanism to produce a comprehensive score for the Medication Pair. The proposed framework is specifically designed for the Medication Pair Prediction task but possesses broader applications in Entity Relation Classification tasks. The efficacy of the proposed framework is demonstrated through superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art approaches, particularly when utilizing OHSMCP, a carefully constructed dataset of Medication Pairs derived from a large-scale OHSSummary Electronic Health Records dataset. The results indicate an improved F1 score of 0.759, surpassing the best existing baseline score of 0.747.

The proposed generalization of the Itô-Wentzell formula accounts for the simultaneous rough movement of a domain's boundary and its internal points, building on existing concepts while overcoming their limitations. A key feature involves representing the boundary and interior points through a unified framework that admits singular control, specifically Heavier side Brownian motion. This development enables a rough version of the parabolic equation to be solved, even when it contains a rough source term and needs to satisfy a condition that combines Cauchy and Dirichlet types, known as a mixed Cauchy-Dirichlet condition. This is achieved by utilizing a combination of recent breakthroughs in rough path theory and novel technical arguments.

A significant challenge in Federated Learning is when aggregated models are deployed to various environments, as they often encounter data distributions that differ significantly. This results in increased learning difficulties and often yields poor performance. To rectify this issue, we introduce an innovative approach known as Random Stroll Learning, which allows the model to adaptively learn multiple distinct data distributions by utilizing bigram transitions, all while preserving user privacy. Building upon this framework, we integrate Random Stroll Learning into the Federated Setting, proposing the "Stroll" algorithm. To demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness, we simulate diverse data environments using bigram tables and show through thorough experiments that it successfully learns to navigate and learn from various data distributions without compromising model privacy.

This research provides a computational verification of the predicted energy spectrum behavior in three-dimensional inertial wave turbulence. Specifically, we determine the scale-dependent inertial wave spectrum, E(k~), and demonstrate its alignment with the proposed relationship, where the spectrum decays according to an exponential function, k~ / k~. k~ and k~ are respectively defined as unknown and unknown. k~ denotes the wavenumber, and k~ is an unknown that can be expressed as an function of several variables, including the wavenumber (k~), and several other unknowns.

This research focuses on examining the influence of mandated mental wellness counseling on the rehabilitation and reintegration of criminal justice system members into society. A quantitative analysis was conducted using data from financial transaction reports, focusing on the outcomes of property crimes. Transactions were analyzed based on the presence or absence of mandated mental wellness counseling. Results indicate that mandated therapy significantly improves the likelihood of individuals resuming their criminal activity and finding employment. These positive effects are more notable among female criminals and those with smaller initial financial transactions. Moreover, mandated therapy has distinct impacts on different crime categories, with the most substantial reduction in recidivism observed in crimes related to drugs.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation is the severe lack of fully annotated images. To tackle this, semi-supervised learning has been widely adopted, leveraging partially labeled images. One promising approach, consistency regularization, generates pseudo-labels for these partially annotated images. However, the effectiveness of this technique relies heavily on the accuracy of the pseudo-labels. We observe that neighboring pixels with differing pseudo-label boundaries often lead to inaccurate consistency regularization losses. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel, straightforward method: filtering out inconsistent regularization losses based on the agreement between pseudo-labels and their transformations. Our proposed approach significantly enhances existing semi-supervised segmentation models, notably boosting O-accuracy by 3.75% on the MR17 dataset for whole brain segmentation with only 12 labeled images. Moreover, it also boosts O-accuracy on the Cardiac segmentation dataset from 77.3% to 79.3% with 20 labeled images. All experiments and models are made publicly available at https://github.com/cjy2017/ACS.

The ATLAS Jet Trigger System must efficiently identify prominent jets in the ATLAS detector while removing unneeded data. Previously, its primary component, the Jet Finding Algorithm (JFA), utilized FPGAs from the Virtex-4 series, which are known for having limited processing power and poor scalability. As the ATLAS detector's data load increases, the V4 FPGAs are now incapable of meeting the V0 specification standards set by the CLIC project. To overcome this obstacle, the AFA algorithm has been redesigned to take advantage of the Ultrascale+ FPGA's advanced features. The new design is based on the Xilinx Ultrascale+ family of chips, which offer higher speed and better scalability. The new AFA design is expected to have around 350 times more performance than the old one, while taking up only about 1.5 times the number of Ultrascale+ FPGA slices. The new AFA is also compatible with the existing ATLAS detector system, thanks to its use of the Aurora protocol for efficient data transfer.

This paper presents a unique method called Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR) that falls under the NER family. ANR is designed to establish a one-to-one connection between an actor's body and a target person's appearance through a neural transformation. Unlike previous approaches, ANR allows for natural movement of the actor while maintaining a precise match of proportions. To achieve this, ANR utilizes a shared skeletal structure for both the actor and the target person, incorporating a specific type of joint rotation. This unique design simplifies the interpretation of poses and enables accurate estimation of body proportions during pose transfers. As a result, ANR outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in static and dynamic scenarios, offering superior performance while being computationally efficient.

A significant obstacle in scientific research on complex systems is distinguishing between true chaos and apparent chaos that arises from limited data or simple, nonchaotic, disordered systems. To tackle this challenge, we have developed a novel, data-driven approach that analyzes the dynamics of an isolated atom subject to continuous laser excitation, which can lead to both chaotic and nonchaotic outcomes. To accurately label the chaotic and nonchaotic dynamics of this system, we have employed a graph neural network and analyzed its operations to pinpoint the underlying mechanism, which comprises three components: a state representation, a chaos detector, and a causal explanation of how the state representation influences the chaos detector through an intermediate explanatory variable, effectively capturing a comprehensive framework for atomic chaos. Furthermore, we have created a user-friendly interactive tool that facilitates examination of this atomic chaos through visualization of the state representation, chaos detection, and causal explanation, which can be observed as we gradually vary a key control parameter and watch the system transition from a nonchaotic to chaotic state and back again.

Evaluating the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean or variance of individual components in a complex distribution, especially when the composition of the distribution is unknown, is a significant challenge in likelihood inference. This issue is particularly prevalent in scenarios where sampling from the intricate distribution is unfeasible but sampling from its simpler components is possible. To tackle this problem, we have introduced a novel approach that involves creating artificial samples by combining the estimates and standard errors of the simple components, likely to accurately assess the plausibility of hypothetical values for the target parameter. As demonstrated in our analysis and simulated scenarios, this method is more accurate and yields unbiased results in comparison to traditional methods.

Deep learning models based on knowledge tracing are particularly effective at
predicting student performance on test questions. However, their
interpretability remains largely obscure. Numerous explainable AI techniques
have been developed to address this issue, yet there's still a gap in
establishing reliable evaluations for their validity and generalizability. To
facilitate rigorous testing and consistent evaluation, we have developed PyKT,
a Python-based framework that not only unifies diverse tracing models but also
provides tools for assessing their reliability through re-conversion metrics,
student performance assessments, and preference learning. Building on pyKT's
capabilities, our research aims to explore the validity and limitations of
these deep learning based tracing models.

Given a compact infinite-dimensional variety $X$, we consider a second-order elliptic operator $P$ associated with a symmetric tensor field, and demonstrate that the closure of $P$'s image equals the set of smooth functions on $X$ that are orthogonal to the kernel of $P$. This result is a direct analogue to the Freidlin-Korner theorem. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this theorem and the density of $P$'s image within the set of functions with compact support in the context of infinite-dimensional flat spaces.

This extended abstract explains the design and development of Alethe, a tool for automating mathematical reasoning. Alethe is developing an adaptable proof framework that accommodates proofs from various other automated reasoning tools. To integrate multiple reasoning engines, Alethe employs a layer of macro expansions. Furthermore, the integration of coinductive constructs into higher-order logic has been achieved through a combination of a custom syntax and a set of macro rules. Additionally, reasoning about unbounded data structures in TCS has been possible through the use of a set of macro transformation rules that convert their semantics into that of a three-valued higher-order logic.

Federated learning enables the collaborative training of machine learning models by multiple users who are connected to a shared server, utilizing their local data. This approach has been successfully applied in various scenarios, including the training of language models, machine learning models, and even artificialRecharge systems. Although several proposals have involved federated learning setups, they have generally been limited to synchronized methods that require the direct comparison of hypothesis states. In contrast, our work is focused on an asynchronous, unconstrained environment, where participants can contribute to the direct training of the model through their own local data. This allows for more flexible and flexible collaborations among parties who may not necessarily be working towards a common goal, but are connected to the same server via the internet. Our work involves the development of a novel learning algorithm that utilizes an accumulated data buffer to facilitate direct, buffer-based comparisons, which is proven to achieve a similar optimal performance rate to conventional federated learning methods under certain mathematical conditions.

End-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems, notably those based on attention mechanisms, have outperformed previous methods by a significant margin. However, these models demand vast amounts of training data. In contrast, systems utilizing speaker lists or large-vocabulary models can achieve high accuracy with relatively small datasets but fall behind when plenty of data is available. Taking advantage of both approaches involves initial training on a small dataset using the former method, followed by joint training with real data including the systems' list-models. To facilitate this transfer, it's crucial to prevent the coarse models from degrading the performance of the detailed neural model. This study investigates various transfer learning strategies, including those across language barriers. It found that contrasting the coarse models' outputs with the fine model's targets enables beneficial transfer, resulting in performance gains of up to 15 words per hour in monolingual settings and 25 words per hour in cross-language scenarios.

Graph neural networks excel at converting complex structural information into compact node node vectors, which is crucial for various downstream tasks like node classification and clustering. To test how well different node vector methods preserve a graph's structure and reflect nodes' roles, the development of suitable evaluation datasets has been scarce. We introduce Twitch Players, an extensive dataset consisting of 14 million edges and 900 thousand nodes, which Anontsachara Schoolkitawat's work focused on representing graph nodes effectively using different neural models. Twitch Players is among the largest datasets in dynamic graph domains, facilitating the assessment of how well the node representation techniques capture the essential structure and role of nodes in graphs.

Our study reveals that previous research on the $f_X(1500)$ resonance in the BaBar dataset may have been confused with the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  Using theoretical predictions validated by analysis of relevant decay datasets such as $B\to \pi KK$, we find that the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance should have a significant signature.  However, such a signature is notably missing in the available data.  On the other hand, the $f_X(1500)$ resonance is predicted to have a small but detectable signature.  Given the detailed predictions generated, future experiments with higher data collection such as the BESIII dataset will have the capability to more accurately determine the nature of the resonance at the $\rho^0(1450)$ mass peak in the relevant invariant mass distributions.

If the dark substance contained a substantial amount of primorial black holes, a specific property of such black holes - with masses in a range where evaporation via Hawking radiation enables the emission of radiation pairs that interact strongly, could potentially threaten the stability of the swampland. Through calculating the probability of such interactions, we can deduce the density of dark substance, which matches recent research within the WMAP-Planck limits. By adjusting the width of the primorial black hole mass range, we can replicate the observed dark substance rotation radius, with the lower limit of this range reflecting evaporative evaporation via gravitational radiation at the end of the radiation period.

An innovative transmission force estimation method is introduced for a series elastic actuator with a compliant transmission, specifically designed to address the issue of force control sensitivity to elastic deformation. By integrating the dynamics of the actuator and applying a stable state estimation technique, the proposed method effectively mitigates the impact of modeling inaccuracies, enabling real-time force control within the elastic range. The method is validated experimentally and shows enhanced performance compared to existing approaches, particularly in terms of precise force control capability.

Self-assembled structures called monolayer rafts form on surfaces when particles with flat faces combine with oil molecules at a water-air interface. These structures can create patterns by overcoming issues that typically hinder self-assembly when the particles are sufficiently large and interactions are balanced. To understand the limits of stability in rafts, we investigate the behavior of rigid particles that form these structures. Using theory and simulation, it is discovered that defects in the surrounding particles can cause a particle to flip over, while the presence of five-fold symmetry can lead to a particle to be left isolated, thus generating faults in the arrangement. These insights help to map out the boundaries of rafts that exhibit five-fold symmetry and may guide the design of particles that form defect-minimized structures when they assemble into rafts.

This research explores a range of gauge theories in three-dimensional space, based on SU(Nc) symmetry, that include a variety of scalar fields with self-interacting potentials of multiple types. We analyze the relationship between these models and their corresponding 'Higgs' phases, evaluating the mass characteristics of model parameters through numerical simulations using a Monte Carlo method. Our analysis also considers the influence of all possible breaking and confining states on the phase chart, which is particularly relevant for quantum chromodynamics in three-dimensional space. Additionally, we have identified several distinct sectors in the phase chart for Nc=2, spanning from fully broken to partially broken configurations, while Nc>=3 displays only fully broken sectors with two distinct regions within the fully broken sector in a specific parameter arrangement.

An autonomous marine robot is to navigate in changing environmental conditions and uncharted territories. A key factor impeding this navigation is the shifting ocean currents that vary with location and time. To address this, we've developed a novel model that accurately captures the changing currents in locations the robot hasn't visited, allowing it to accurately predict conditions in new areas. This model enables the robot to efficiently learn about the ocean currents and their conditions. By utilizing a sparse Gaussian process in the time domain, we've achieved a high level of model accuracy with a minimal amount of data, thus improving navigation speeds. The model's performance has been demonstrated to accurately predict currents with a low RMSE of 0.13 m/s and allows the robot to navigate effectively, as shown in our experimental results.

Binary decision trees are commonly employed to represent functions with multiple binary inputs, however, they are inefficient at scaling for functions that involve many inputs due to their depth increasing linearly. In contrast, arrangement networks are an effective method for simple tasks by achieving constant-time solutions through a linear increase in wire count. The drawback of arrangement networks is their difficulty in modification to accommodate additional input variables, resulting in an exponential wire requirement. This paper presents a novel class of binary decision networks called arrangement networks that are characterized by their wire efficiency and constant depth, providing a effective solution for functions that involve a moderate to high number of inputs, including combinatorial sorting and network congestion problems.

We employ a semi-rigorous method to find exact solutions to the Einstein field equations, representing a dual-fluid star composed of an anisotropic fluid and a fluid with isotropic pressure. The model incorporates rotating objects and derives key parameters, including mass, via a matching process at the object's surface. A specific equation of state is used to illustrate the model's capabilities, with further analysis focusing on verifying the stability of the obtained solutions using standard physical criteria.

We've created a statistical model to examine the spiral patterns in a galaxy similar to the Milky Way, using about 50,000 near-infrared data points from the Milky Way. Our analysis reveals that the galaxy's spiral arms consist of multiple helices at different radii, with some helices showing more distinct vertical patterns than others. We discover that the vertical patterns of these helices are influenced by the galaxy's vertical frequency, with certain patterns matching those predicted by the epicyclical theory. Some vertical patterns cannot be fully explained by this theory and may indicate the presence of dark matter. The study also highlights the importance of studying the spiral patterns in the vertical dimension to gain deeper insights into the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy.

Galactic mergers and linear structure collapses lead to significant changes in how galaxies form, with major combine formations occurring along the paths galaxies take within the cosmos, often associated with dense cosmic web nodes. Understanding the impact of magnetic fields on these large-scale formation processes is currently lacking in both theoretical models and computational simulations. Our study performs large-scale cosmic web simulations that incorporate magnetic field effects, utilizing up to one million particles per simulation to analyze the impact of these fields on galaxy formations forming through large-scale processes. We compared simulations with and without magnetic field influence, observing distinct changes in gas and stellar formations. We found that magnetic fields impact the threshold of turbulence caused by the Jeans length, reducing star-formation rates and impacting galaxy morphologies. This effect is equivalent to a change of 0.3 in cosmic scales, potentially accounting for a significant discrepancy between simulated and actual galaxy formations.

A primary objective of pandemic research is to accelerate the creation of effective medical treatments by closely monitoring the severity of infected individuals, which is typically achieved through manual analysis of electronic health records, a time-consuming and costly process. To accelerate this, we introduce a cutting-edge framework to enhance the efficiency of infection-related tasks, particularly severity classification, utilizing data from suboptimal unlabeled samples. Our approach, named IAMN, integrates a contrastive loss function and a suboptimal data augmentation technique known as Mixup, leveraging hypothetical infection-related sample connections to elevate the accuracy of severity classification. Our experiments utilizing real-world MIMIC-III datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods by a significant margin, improving severity classification accuracy from 71.44% to 74.26%.

Most current systems for correcting grammatical errors rely heavily on large amounts of annotated data within a specific domain. A significant limitation exists as these models often fail to correct errors in new, unseen domains without additional fine-tuning. This research proposes a novel approach using low-shot domain-transferable meta-grammatical error correction via extra-curricular extra-model learning. This multi-layered approach initially trains an initial system to identify and correct specific errors, such as those found in the Fredroid domain. Subsequently, a second, autonomous system automatically generates synthetic data from various other domains, enriching the initial training dataset. A final meta-learning model is then trained on this combined dataset, significantly enhancing the model's ability to accurately correct errors in unseen domains with very limited target domain data. A pilot study validates the efficacy of this approach, demonstrating its potential for achieving high accuracy in correcting grammatical errors in unseen domains with as little as 50 training samples per domain.

This study develops a statistical framework to accurately interpret rounded numerical data in finite populations. 
We establish an analytical model and conduct simulations to closely examine the ambiguity present in such data. 
Our results reveal that ignoring this uncertainty can significantly distort estimates of key population metrics, including totals, means, and coefficients of variation. 
In fact, we find that accounting for ambiguity yields much more precise confidence intervals than traditional methods that overlook this uncertainty. 
As an alternative, we introduce a new approach that simultaneously captures the entire range of possible values represented by rounded observations. 
This new method can be utilized to create confidence intervals based on either the original observations or the underlying values before rounding occurs. 
To demonstrate the practical value of our framework, we apply it to empirical examples, involving spending estimates from a survey of museums in the U.S. as well as patient age assessments in the U.S. conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Researchers investigated the magnetic behavior and electronic structure of single-crystal GdInO$_3$ through various experiments including neutron diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and optical transmission spectroscopy. The results indicate that GdInO$_3$ exhibits a two-fold degenerate electronic state in its $4f$ shell, with effective Sander's sums of $1.56$ for the $4f^{7}$ configuration and $2.78$ for the $5d^1$ configuration, consistent with spin-triplet hybridization. Additionally, the study employed a centered honeycomb lattice to describe the magnetic structure of Gd, which forms triangular and triangularly frustrated sublattices. A Heisenberg-Hafner model was then developed to model this structure, suggesting that long-range magnetic order is established by the Heisenberg interaction, while short-range correlations are formed through the Hafner interaction. The exchange-bohr radius calculated for GdInO$_3$ indicates a significant impact of the Hafner interaction on its low-temperature properties.

This work examines the distribution of non-transferable goods to non-cooperative agents, focusing on two key aspects: the existence of Nash equilibria and fairness in the outcomes of such situations. Our analysis covers various scenarios, taking into account whether agents have a accurate understanding of others' valuations for the goods, and whether their valuations are limited to being monotonic or strictly increasing. We have established the existence of Nash equilibria for several scenarios, including when agents have a accurate understanding of each other's valuations for two or more goods. In doing so, we have determined the minimal number of monotonic valuations required to ensure the existence of Nash equilibria in the general case, where agents may have different valuations for the goods. We have also determined that the fairness level of equilibria in scenarios where agents may be aware or unaware of others' valuations can be accurately measured by the Batyrev ratio, and that the fairness level of equilibria in scenarios with potential misinformation can be limited to the same level as the ratio of valuations of the agent who values the goods differently.

Recent research has focused on creating deterministic mappings between domain spaces to reduce variance in domain adaptation models, but this approach may introduce biased transformations that lead to over-smoothed results. To mitigate this issue, we propose introducing stochastic transformations between domain spaces as an alternative. Building on this concept, we develop two new methods for unsupervised manifold domain adjustment: stochastic flow matching and stochastic vector field matching. These new approaches are gifted standalone frameworks, yet they can also serve as complementary components in hybrid architectures that combine deterministic and stochastic transformations. Our results show that incorporating stochastic transformations improves domain adaptation performance, yielding more balanced and realistic domain conversions.

The spiral galaxy UGC 8839 exhibits an unusually high redshift relative to its morphology, which is typical of a normal spiral. This discrepancy is believed to result from the galaxy undergoing a major merger that has yet to fully merge. As a result, the galaxy displays an unusual structure with multiple distinct components, including a highly concentrated central region, a large elliptical disk, and a highly rotated spiral component. Our new multi-wavelength observations, which include data from various wavelengths, allow us to map its hydrogen map and reveal its unusual structure with three separate nuclear regions connected by compact nuclear stalks. These regions, which have different rotational characteristics, are unusual and provide a clear visual representation of galaxy mergers in progress. The central region, which has the highest surface brightness, exhibits a flat rotation curve, which is typical of a spiral galaxy. This, combined with our dynamical mass modeling, allows us to estimate that the central region has a total mass of approximately $1.3 \times 10^9$ solar masses, which is mainly composed of dark matter. The outer regions, including the large elliptical disk, exhibit signs of significant dark matter presence as well. These regions, which are highly enriched with dark matter, provide a clear visual representation of how galaxies can be transformed during the merging process.

This paper discusses the use of paleo-detectors in searching for the dark matter interaction known as spin-dependent scattering. We examine how paleo-detectors can be used to constrain this type of dark matter interaction and calculate their sensitivity in various regions of parameter space.
