Building upon the foundational work of W.R. Reeh and D. Haag in quantum field theory, our analysis focuses on constructing spatially localized observables, which are parameterized by both a wedge-shaped region and a real number. Our construction yields a dense subset within the full algebra of observables and demonstrates that the associated net of algebras shares key properties found in conformal field theory, including unitary and projective representations. A notable outcome of our research is the derivation of a continuous, unitary representation for the modular group of a specific, densely defined subset of the full algebra - a set that is itself localized within a specific one-parameter family of intervals. This localization property was not previously demonstrated to be achievable. Our analysis is rooted in the use of endomorphisms within the framework of von Neumann algebras, which are known for their modular theory. Our research is then extended to include any type III_1 factor, rather than just the algebra associated with the CFT.

The controversy surrounding 5G technology's safety has particularly affected children and teenagers, with concerns stemming from the need for 5G signal dissemination over a broad area, including schools and medical facilities. As a result, it is crucial to determine the extent of 2.1 GHz and 3.5 GHz 5G signal emission from base transmitters, specifically those optimized for maximum coverage, when it comes to passing over populations of children, schools, hospitals, and other areas. This study is focused on investigating how much of these signals are actually transmitted when 5G towers, operating with maximum coverage, are positioned above children, schools, hospitals, and towns with populations under 18 years of age. It is important to note that not all 5G signals are harmful, but rather only the higher frequency signals, namely 2.1 GHz and 3.5 GHz, which are used for maximum coverage. As revealed in this study, the majority of areas are unaffected by these signals, with over nine out of ten times passing over children, schools, hospitals, and towns with populations under 18 years of age actually showing no emission. Consequently, it is inferred that locating 5G towers in unoccupied areas is still preferable, despite the fact that their signal is transmitted on lower frequency channels.

This research paper formulates a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation for deep-water gravity waves, characterized by consistent vorticity. The Dysthe equation, derived from a Hamiltonian formulation, represents an approximation of the fully non-linear water wave problem under specific conditions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between Dysthe's equation and the fully non-linear problem by analyzing the convergence rates, identifying how vorticity plays a role in determining convergence within a specific timeframe.

We propose a novel framework for differential geometry on locally convex spaces,
focusing on simplicity and clarity while maintaining rigorous mathematical foundations.
Our approach allows for a re-examination of key concepts from differential geometry,
including the Stokes theorem, through this lens. Additionally, we introduce a modified
version of the Stokes theorem that incorporates both vector fields with compact support
and distributional forms.

Autonomous mobile robots depend on path planning systems to move from one location to another. These systems are often supplemented with sonar blending algorithms that utilize data from sonar sensors to create a smooth, layered navigation map. While existing sonar blending methods are effective, they tend to be overly complex, computationally expensive, or lack the ability to process data quickly. In contrast, our proposed immediate sonar blending method is simple to execute but produces results of comparable quality. Our new method can produce similar outcomes to established schemes but with the added benefit of very fast computation times, typically under 10 milliseconds. Our method is also versatile enough to be used with a range of sonar blending approaches, making it suitable for layers of navigation managers that integrate multiple sonar sensors. Our results show that our immediate sonar blending method can create high-quality paths that are difficult to distinguish from those created by more established methods, even in complex scenarios with obstacles and narrow passages.

The amount of information on breaking news has significantly increased with the widespread adoption of social media, resulting in many users having difficulty distinguishing between true stories and fabricated ones. This problem is compounded by the fact that identifying fake news often requires a deep understanding of multiple related stories, which can be challenging for average users. To tackle this issue, we explored the potential of using automatic text summarization models to enhance the performance of Fake/BrealNews datasets. Specifically, we utilized two summarization models to generate concise versions of both real and fake news articles, which were then utilized as input features for a BERT-based classifier. The use of these summaries yielded a notable improvement of 7% in classification performance compared to the existing baseline.

This research investigates the local intensity of great circles with positive radius of curvature within the space of unit-norm complex-valued functions, denoted as L2(S1), that form a Gaussian random field. Focus is placed on understanding how the curvature of a great circle influences the rate at which it converges, measured in terms of its radius of curvature R. Under specific technical conditions, the study establishes the exact order of this convergence, revealing that the local density approaches a singular behavior near points where the circle intersects other geometric features, aligning with findings from a previously related work by Constable et al. (1987). The research also provides the influence of this curvature on the local density within the space of real-valued functions, denoted as gRF. The investigation extends to understanding the small-probability behavior of randomly oriented great circles that satisfy certain threshold conditions, and the results demonstrate the role of this curvature in determining the conditional distribution function and the conditional mean field of these circles.

The implementation of Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) has been accelerated by 5G systems, yet its attractive efficiency comes with increased vulnerability to malicious users. We examined a 5G NOMA system where an eavesdropper is capable of tampering with signals and injecting fake messages into the downlink channel. Our focus was on preventing a specific attack where the attacker tries to deceive two nominal receivers into allowing a malicious user to inject fake commands, which could be pre-programmed into user devices. By analyzing the characteristics of legitimate nominal users, we developed a method to allow two nominal receivers to distinguish malicious signals from genuine ones through a deciphering process. To overcome the challenge posed by a attacker who can listen in on the entire communication, we proposed a new ciphering technique that utilizes a fraction of a receiver's knowledge, demonstrating its reliability through both theoretical analysis and experimental evidence. Our discovery indicates that (25 + $\epsilon$) bits of randomness are necessary for securing a malicious user's attempt in a nominal communication channel (where $\epsilon$ can be an arbitrarily small positive number). Furthermore, we investigated the relationship between a receiver and attacker's processing capabilities and data rates, revealing that our ciphering technique is feasible for typical mobile device processors and slower than Galileo-based malicious users.

Intriguingly, research on using the $\ell_1$-norm for fingerprint identification has been relatively limited, primarily due to its complexity, especially when dealing with rotation invariance. To address this challenge, we develop a simplified model that focuses on binary, one-dimensional, i.i.d. data with rotational invariance. Initially, we demonstrate that the standard NP-hard definition of this problem can be resolved into an equivalent optimization problem by removing the constraint of rotation invariance, however, this solution leads to multiple locally optimal solutions. Subsequently, we introduce a new optimization problem, which is consistent with the original NP-hard definition, possesses a unique optimal solution, and ensures convergence to this solution at a linear rate. Moreover, we develop a straightforward algorithm to achieve this optimal solution. Through numerical simulations, our algorithm displays remarkable efficiency, with results showing significantly improved performance when the distribution variance is relatively large, but with less favorable results in more compact scenarios. To further resolve issues of numerical instability caused by potential singularities of the optimal parameter, we modify the algorithm to converge with a linear rate to an $\varepsilon$-optimal solution.

Semantic Annotation (SemAnn) has greatly facilitated the access to high-quality training data for downstream tasks, yet it acquires limited attention for emotional questions due to its time-consuming nature. With the advent of NLP tools, NLP-supported Emotion Annotation (EmAnn) has been introduced to reduce the burden of manual labeling, yet existing SemAnn frameworks fail to consider emotional questions due to inaccurate bag-of-words assumptions. In contrast, NLP-based annotations incorporate rich semantic information via word-order-aware decoding models. With the prominent BERT-based semantic annotation framework, we integrate it with EmAnn to (1) enhance the annotation accuracy of emotional questions, (2) identify the potential emotional stance of annotators, and (3) utilize human feedback to revise low-confidence annotations. Our experimental results on the Facebook emotion dataset demonstrate significant improvements from the BERT-based SemAnn framework, yielding substantial increases in annotation accuracy of emotional questions and potential emotional stance.

The concept of a power order is built upon a base order by raising its elements to successive integer powers, and this paper investigates the properties of power orders in relation to totally ordered groups and fields. We establish that certain group and field characteristics can be determined through exponential bounds and demonstrate how these bounds are utilized to solve System A, a collection of atomic formulas involving order, and demonstrate that the number of possible solutions for such formulas is finite and can be explicitly ordered. Additionally, the paper shows that given two definable sets, a relationship between their sizes can be determined and that this cannot be achieved for n-ary relations when n is greater than 1.

A new class of magnetic white dwarfs in accreting systems, called asynchronous magnetic polars (AMPs), have been recently identified. Their distinction lies in the rotation of the neutron star and the white dwarf, which rotates asynchronously due to the magnetic braking effect. This new class represents a significant development, as it was only in recent years that asynchronous systems were found in two other compact object binaries involving a neutron star or a black hole. We explored the X-ray spectrum of four AMPs, searching for hard spectral components often present in other polar spectra. We found that asynchronous systems indeed exhibit harder X-ray spectra compared to their non-asynchronous counterparts, similar to findings in another two asynchronous systems. We found evidence of an X-ray disk component above the Epstein curve, which is typically observed in normal polars but not in intermediate polar spectra. This curve may be attributed to the shift in flow regime from supersonic to subsonic due to the higher values of the Reynolds number in intermediate polars. The presence of this hard spectrum also indicates evidence for X-ray radiation pressure-driven winds, which are commonly observed in normal polars but not always in intermediate polars.

This research presents an innovative reduced basis method for resolving fluid-structure interaction problems. The method is designed to handle multiple problems with varying domains by utilizing a separate reduced basis technique for the structure, in contrast to the previous single reduced basis approach for the whole domain. The method employs a looser coupling strategy, where the previous monolithic high-fidelity approach is replaced by a sequential all-at-once reduced basis method. Although the reduced basis method has some disadvantages, such as potential non-convergence, the method is made more flexible with the partitioned approach. However, this comes with an increased computational cost of $O(N^{0.5})$ rather than $O(N)$, in accordance with the underlying numerical method for fluid dynamics. The method is further developed by combining the existing single and previous multi-domain reduced basis techniques.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate independently, they need an effective layout representation that's easy to interpret and facilitate path planning. Current research into layout representations has primarily focused on content aspects, with less attention given to the spatial organization component. To supplement existing content-centric approaches, we introduce a spatial organization module that uses a hierarchical graph to represent the topological layout. This hierarchical graph captures the spatial arrangement of environmental objects, allowing for more efficient navigation. By integrating this topological layout representation with current methods, our approach demonstrates significant improvements in navigation performance in unknown settings, as evidenced by our experiments in simulated and real-world environments.

This document describes the proposed system for the "Identifying Aggressive Tweets" task in SemEval-2019 Challenge 6, where participants evaluate the language used in approximately 35,000 tweets to determine their level of aggression. The challenge dataset consists of three categories labeling each tweet as non-aggressive, moderately aggressive, or highly aggressive.

Our system has a unique advantage of having access to the complete test dataset, which is not provided in the challenge. This extra data was used for additional experimentation. Two versions of the proposed system are described, including a baseline deep learning model based on BERT, and a challenging classifier combining ELM and LiNGSTFS with careful feature engineering. Neither deep learning models nor classical machine learning models are mutually exclusive, and each system has its strengths, leading to our outcome of ensembling these approaches.

Employing atomic interferometry in combination with the Meissner effect can achieve extraordinary precision in measuring local magnetic field changes. By taking advantage of superconducting films' ability to expel magnetic fields and show large, quantized shifts in the atomic interference patterns, this method is capable of detecting minute alterations down to 10$^{-15}$ G / $\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ at 1Hz bandwidth. This sensitivity is 4 orders of magnitude greater than what can be attained through traditional magnetometry methods using SQUIDs or spin precession, and relies on 4 times the atomic density. The procedure is fully passively damped, thus eliminating the need for complex systems to suppress vibrations. Although initially demonstrated with optical trapping of atoms, the approach is also applicable to gas-based atomic interferometry.

We've utilized first-principles calculations to investigate the spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect (MPMCE) in two-dimensional (2D) MoS2, employing the within-density functional theory (DWFT) methodology. Inorganic compounds MoS2 exhibit significant closure of the direct and indirect band gaps caused by DWFT. Notably, MoS2 shows large, positive change in entropy near its direct gap closure, providing a foundation for investigating MPMCE within this material. By applying an external magnetic field along the c-axis of MoS2, we observed unprecedented zero-field entropy at 5K, indicating the potential presence of local field-induced MPMCE at low temperatures. Furthermore, we found that applying a 10eV hydrogen potential to MoS2 can induce field-free 5K local entropy change, suggesting the potential for achieving field-free MPMCE within this 2D material.

This research investigates the impact of electron spill-over and nonlocality on gap-plasmons in nano-gaps, particularly in limits where the gap size approaches zero. To model this, a nonlocal generalization of the random phase approximation was employed. Our results reveal that electron spill-over significantly influences gap-plasmon mode localization, causing a red-shift in mode frequencies, a phenomenon absent in local models. Furthermore, the 2D approximation of electron spill-over leads to inaccurate predictions, resulting in additional mode frequencies. These outcomes are anticipated to influence the design of 2D electron-spill-over models and their applicability in nano-gaps.

The addition of normal forms to the Calculus of Constructions with Inductive
Types, specifically extended with the Prop sort, would significantly compromise its proof irrelevance property. As a consequence, robust normalization techniques have been developed. Notable examples include K-norm and weak-head normal form, though their limitations lie in not being human-readable. As an alternative, this work introduces a novel, intuitive normalization strategy, called the robust long normal form, which maintains the integrity of term equalities while incorporating additional congruence rules to preserve proof irrelevance. Empirical findings reveal that this approach, when applied to the Coq kernel, yields normal forms for a majority of terms, specifically 93% in random terms and 81% in the Coq Library.

To provide an intuitive understanding of topological quantum phenomena, we've created educational tools that simplify complex ideas, focusing on the 1D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By analyzing this system, we can examine the particle transport properties of its boundary states, utilizing the concept of topological charge within a drive-drape protocol. Our study also explores the role of disorder in a variety of random instances. Additionally, we've developed tools to visualize the topological aspects of the model in its generalized version, including a tensor network representation of the driven system and an automatic method for creating visualization graphs. These developments will serve as a foundation for creating similar educational resources for other topological models.

We have developed a continuous geometric framework to model dependencies within a probability space, which aligns with both finite mixtures and a broader class of models. This framework utilizes geometry and geometry-based measures, which have the capability to represent dependent structures organically. We will demonstrate how this framework can be employed to analyze a model of interest, provide a case study involving spatial percolation, and discuss the advantages of adopting this geometry-based approach for model development and comparison purposes.

Using the dual-loop method, researchers calculated the two-loop dual supergravity predictions for four-point correlators of BPS operators within $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory, specifically focusing on the IR divergent terms. A key finding is that the dual supergravity results fail to account for certain terms proportional to $\pi^4$ that were initially thought to be canceled out due to the dual-loop approximation. These uncancelled terms become relevant at odd values of $n$ when considering operators with complex phases, contradicting recent finite N^2 conformal field theory computations. The findings indicate that the dual supergravity computations are incomplete and suggest a need for revised methods to accurately capture the dynamics at odd values of $n$. The researchers leverage their results to predict specific values for coefficients of dual supergravity in the expansion of anomalous dimensions for operators with specific values of $J$, which can be tested against numerical data for the full anomalous dimensions. Additionally, the dual supergravity computations yield specific values for the first two coefficients in the $1/J$ expansion of the phase of anomalous dimensions for odd values of $n$ greater than or equal to three.

High-performance computing on SIMD/GPUs has a limited number of threads, causing them to compete for memory and potentially disrupt the coalescing of global accesses. This issue is particularly problematic in large-scale applications on GPU clusters, where developers often rely on global arrays for efficiency despite their drawbacks in terms of scalability and memory capacity. To address this challenge, we introduced DynaSOAr, a novel concurrent memory allocator designed with lock-free structures that minimize atomic operations and ensure thread safety. Our evaluation results show significant reductions in global memory access times, with further improvements expected on larger scales and at even higher frequencies.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse class of sublinear operators along with their commutators when mapping from generalized mixed Morrey spaces to either the same space or Lebesgue spaces. Additionally, novel sufficient conditions are derived for the boundedness of these operators and their commutators, including those associated with the maximal operator, Calderon-Zygmund singular integral operator, potential operator, and sublinear operator T.

Using a first-principles approach based on initial principles of relativistic theory, we examine the total magnetic anisotropy energy of an Mn adatom and Mn dimer on the Nb(110) surface, including the exchange interaction between the Mn defect and Nb substrate. We derive the exchange spectral function and analyze how the local spin magnetic anisotropy spectrum is related to the Nb surface electronic density of states. Notably, we find that the local spin magnetic anisotropy at specific energy points can be directly related to the atomic orbital composition of the corresponding electron states. Our theoretical model successfully predicts the total magnetic anisotropy by integrating the local spin magnetic anisotropy over a range of energy.

Our proposed FourierMask presents a significant improvement over FourierField's instance segmentation capabilities. By enhancing the multi-instance encoding FourierField lacks, FourierMask integrates this encoding into each individual object. Building upon FourierField's successful deception of image generation through implicit mapping, FourierMask achieves even more realistic results in single-object scenarios, leveraging a condition-specific transformation for precise segmentation.

Let $M$ be a compact, oriented surface with the boundary consisting of $k$ disjoint components. If $M$ has genus $g$ and each boundary component $\gamma_i$ has a specified orientation, then $M$ can be embedded in three-dimensional space such that all boundary components are homotopically equivalent to the same closed curve in the range of the embedding if and only if the genus of $M$ does not exceed the linking number of the curve with itself. Additionally, if $M$ admits a locally convex immersion whose boundary components are all homotopically equivalent to the same closed curve, then $M$ can be deformed into the boundary components of a convex surface while maintaining the same boundary conditions, provided that the genus of $M$ is zero, or $M$ can be deformed into the boundary components of a knotted torus while maintaining the same boundary conditions, provided that the genus of $M$ is one.

Our research employs satellite polarization polarization data from MODIS and MISR to develop a technique for identifying the veiled core within opaque convective clouds using chemical tracers. A statistical analysis of cloud features identified the veiled structure as an area of increased linear polarization within a cloud's dark, highly retro-illuminated center. Despite its name, the veiled core can appear as a lighter patch within a cloud. By combining polarization data with a machine learning algorithm, we found that the veiled core is associated with localized decreases in backscatter and a specific range of orientation angles. A case study using MISR and MODIS data revealed that the veiled core in cloud T86 over the Atlantic is caused by a localized increase in sulfur dioxide gas thickness.

To counteract gradual gravitational dominance from galactic centers, space colonies located on the periphery of galaxies must utilize high-speed propulsion systems like relativistic self-induced translucency (R.S.I.T.). Ion propulsion systems, while efficient for sustained travel, are insufficient for making up lost ground due to their thrust limitations. A solution lies in employing a chirping ramp rate for their power systems, gradually increasing their speed over time to overcome gravitational forces and allow for productive travel within galaxy structures.

To characterize additional systems like TOI-712, we've discovered a planetary ensemble consisting of four planets. This pair of planets, b and c, are small and reside outside the stellar neighborhood, while planet d is located within the habitable zone. The system's stars exhibit unusual activity, yet have low overall activity levels. Furthermore, careful analysis revealed no significant discrepancies in the planets' orbital paths, indicating a relatively stable system dynamic. TOI-712 is among the youngest discovered systems with a diverse planetary population outside of the inner rocky planet realm.

This work focuses on using Carbon and Nitrogen as photosensitizers in TiO2, addressing the issue of their agglomeration within the TiO2 structure. Through first-principles calculations using the VASP package and a range of methods including RPA and U, we examined the stability, magnetic properties, and conductivity of doped TiO2. Our results suggest that while Carbon and Nitrogen can indeed be physisorbed onto the TiO2 surface, they may exhibit unexpected agglomeration behavior, and that considering agglomerated structures is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of their electronic and magnetic arrangement.

This letter describes the challenge of detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider when one of the top-quarks decays into a bottom quark and the W-boson is produced in the elastic mode. To overcome this difficulty, we suggest using an all-embracing strategy to analyze the data and thus extract the production cross-section of this difficult process. We then specifically examine the case where the other top-quark decays into three charged jets, and determine the necessary criteria to filter out the background noise from other processes. We also discuss the potential to distinguish the characteristic signature of bottom quarks in this process with current detectors at the LHC.

Our investigation into the turbulent intra-cluster medium (ICM) continues, focusing on how ICM structure functions relate to each other. In our previous research using simulated X-ray data, we found that compressive ICM turbulence affects the power-law patterns in these structure functions. To further understand this relationship, we need to accurately measure ICM structure functions across various scales. However, current measurements are influenced inaccuracies from neighboring pixels in X-ray images, potentially altering the intended patterns. This study analyzes the impact of these measurement errors, particularly in the context of the imaged region's size. Our findings indicate that errors due to neighboring pixels can overestimate structure functions for small scales and underestimate them for larger scales, regardless of the presence of turbulence. Utilizing a statistical model, we can forecast these errors, allowing us to accurately compare observed ICM structure functions with simulated turbulent data. This adjusted comparison may reveal the underlying turbulent characteristics of the ICM from their structure functions.

A Ramsey property is identified when every two-coloring of a graph's edges yields a specific monochromatic subgraph. We explore this concept in relation to infinite graph components, defining an $\infty$-Ramsey property based on monochromatic subgraphs of a particular type. Our research reveals that certain infinite components possess this $\infty$-Ramsey property, but not all do, and we establish conditions and counterexamples to characterize those that do possess the property.

The complex structure within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) remains a mystery due to its diverse molecular features, driven by a significant gravitational influence from the Galactic Centre. This gravitational pull is thought to be affected by the gravitational features within the nucleus itself, however, its rotational nature makes precise measurements difficult. One method utilized to analyze molecular configurations involves 2D statistical tools such as projection scalar parameters or anisotropic spatial correlations known as 2D correlation functions. Through the analysis of near-infrared to sub-millimeter wavelength data of the CMZ, specifically using the Spitzer Infrared Celestial Map (IRAS) and the Sub-millimeter Arcminute Excursion (SAGE), a strong correlation was found between dust and molecular lines, displaying a distinct elliptical pattern aligned with the Galactic disc. This correlation, known as the 2D correlation function, indicates the presence of linear molecular structures often referred to as "flows". Despite some limitations, this study provides the most comprehensive analysis of 2D correlations at a large scale, utilizing a scale of 100 parsecs, which is critical for understanding the overall nuclear mass configuration. Furthermore, this study is essential in preparing for the upcoming data from the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), however, further observations are needed to understand the gas dynamics, which is crucial for completing the preparation.

A significant number of video accessibility tools are available to assist individuals with disabilities in understanding video content. However, none of these tools specifically target patients with Bell's paralysis, who suffer from facial muscle weakness on one side of their face. Although medical professionals use video consultations to assess the condition, they also face challenges with time constraints and traffic when in-person appointments are necessary. To address this challenge, we created a detection system for Bell's paralysis that focuses on video eye movement analysis. By utilizing state-of-the-art eye detection and machine learning techniques, our system can identify the presence of Bell's paralysis by comparing eye movement patterns, specifically the distance between eyes and eye movement speed, between normals and patients. We tested our system on a diverse set of 70 videos, consisting of 35 normal and 35 patient videos, and achieved a 97.14% accuracy rate in eye movement extraction, ultimately resulting in 94.29% accuracy in detecting Bell's paralysis. Furthermore, our system is efficient enough to process videos at a rate of 312.85 milliseconds per video using 8GB of RAM and a CPU CPU Intel Core i5 8th Gen.

In the lattice QED framework, Qutrit-based qSOAP has demonstrated capability in identifying both topological and non-topological sounds. Our analysis of sQED reveals the origin of these sounds, involving discrete non-topological enhancements due to finite qutrit dynamics and continuous topological sounds linked to the lattice's geometric properties. These non-topological sounds may interfere with the detection of the Chern-Simons effect, whereas the continuous topological sounds seem compatible. Further investigations are needed to understand the impact of these sounds on full lattice QED.

Our analysis indicates that strongly interacting electrons within the micrometer-thick sections of laser-prepared metal targets can lead to the generation of linearly polarized photons when subjected to intense lasers. These electrons must be moving at speeds close to the speed of light. If these targets are then bombarded with a second linearly polarized laser, the resulting dense cloud will contain large numbers of positrons with maintained spin alignment, specifically up to $10^{20}$ at frequencies of $10\omega_0$, where $\omega_0$ represents the laser frequency. This substantial production of positrons can be achieved through a process called linearly polarized laser-induced pair production, and they will be ejected along the target's normal vector at relativistic speeds. These highly populated, spin-aligned positrons possess the necessary conditions for conducting comprehensive research into the complex behavior of antimatter under the influence of strong magnetic fields and for the development of next-generation, particle-like sources of purified positron beams.

Building on prior research, several scholars have sought to prove that the maximum diameter of a non-amenable finite group is logarithmic relative to its largest irreducible character degree. We strengthen this hypothesis by demonstrating that the maximum diameter of a non-amenable finite group is logarithmic relative to the square root of its largest irreducible character degree. Additionally, we examine several families of non-amenable finite groups and determine their diameter in relation to their largest irreducible character degree, including groups of affine, projective affine, and M2-type. These analyses help refine an estimate for the bound of diameter mentioned in a prior study.

This research focuses on the development of a temperature sensor with high precision and minimal power consumption, capable of detecting minute temperature changes. An optimized subthreshold circuit is designed to detect temperature changes as small as 0.24°C with low distortion and a compact form factor occupying just 0.016$mm^2$. The proposed analyzer operates within a wide supply range (0.6V to 1.8V) and consumes only 12µW at 1.2V, achieving a temperature sensing error of 1.4°C and a conversion time of 11ms. Furthermore, the analyzer's performance remains consistent across varying supply voltages, as demonstrated in simulations.

Long-lived stellar magnetic fields require a non-radial configuration, even in stars that lack rotation. Typically, magnetic fields within stars display both radial and non-radial components. For a steady state, the dominant component should be the non-radial one. This can be accomplished through a specific initial condition or by the gradual development of the non-radial component via resistive processes. Here, a mathematical model is one in which the dominant magnetic component could be the radial one. However, further analysis indicates that this model is unstable across all frequencies. Consequently, this outcome leads to rapid transformation of the radial magnetic field into a tangled configuration, regardless of the presence of convection within the star. It should be noted that these findings may have implications for understanding the long-lived magnetic fields observed in Ap-stars.

We develop a novel numerical method to solve the time-dependent Ricci flow for probability distributions in a quantum field theory context, which mirrors the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG) approach. This method aligns with recent developments in flow-matching for learning unknown function forms. By transforming the Ricci flow equations into a form suitable for analysis, we can apply techniques from quantum field theory to extract the scale-dependent behavior of a system. When applied to a group of $N$ scalar fields, our method yields results that closely match the established EFT/FRG findings for various system size scenarios. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our method for non-local effects and discuss its potential applications to more complex FRG problems.

Music recommendation systems, including those used in streaming services, have vastly popularized music consumption but still fall short of ideal satisfaction levels. One reason for this is the limited diversity in music discovery, as users often become accustomed to certain styles. To address this issue, our study puts forward a novel concept called the meta recommendation system for music. 

Our research identifies distinct categories of music interest through the analysis of a user's listening history, taking into account elements such as genre, artist, tempo, and musical mode. These elements are utilized to introduce the idea of a 'piper', which represents a diverse set of music that may or may not align with a user's typical listening habits. 

By incorporating the piper into our framework, we leverage machine learning to rank music that surprises and delights users, ultimately introducing two innovative approaches: personalized Piper, which surveys a user's preferences, and Blind Piper, which challenges them. Our findings are supported by a large dataset consisting of 144,519 users' listening histories from Spotify, demonstrating the effectiveness of our system in both confirming and wide-ranging evaluation scenarios.

We are exploring various geometric structures within the framework of Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, likely uncovering an underlying unity. These structures include vector fields, tensor fields, connections, and other geometric concepts.

A dark molecular ridge known as the Dragon NDB, spanning 1.5 kiloparsecs across and located in the Galactic plane, serves as the prototype for dark nebulae. At the center of this formation lies a dense core region, which is 400 parsecs wide and exhibits a distinct dU/dR gradient. This dense core is characterized by an elevated concentration of dust, which suggests the presence of growing stellar embryos, now in their early stages of development. Notably, within this NDB core, we have identified ten dense, dark peaks, each with an elevated concentration of carbon monoxide and submillimeter light. These dense peaks are believed to be in various stages of collapse, with some fully collapsed and others stable, and they comprise nearly 25% of the total mass within this dense core region. Based on infrared and submillimeter observations, the dense core of the Dragon NDB displays the traits of a massive star-forming region, which may be emerging in this dark nebula.

Godel modal logic, based on partial orders, is an extension of Godel first-order logic,
building upon the basis of pre-ordered relations. We have investigated various types of
algebras related to Godel modal logics, based on the relations of partial and pre-orders.
Additionally, we have explored the use of finite Godel algebras. In our research, we
have also discuss T_n and S_n modalities and their corresponding Godel modal logics.
Furthermore, we have shown that every finite pre- and partial order can be represented
using a combination of T_n and S_n pre- and partial order relations. Moreover, we have
established that the relational structures of the corresponding logics can be captured
by n-sorted Kripke frames. Finally, we have demonstrated that the pre- and partial order
relations can be replaced by their n-bivalued counterparts without compromising the
completeness of the corresponding Godel modal logics.

LiDAR point clouds, generated by mobile LiDAR systems on vehicles or drones, play a crucial role in various applications such as visualization, navigation, and LiDAR image reconstruction. With the advancement of artificial intelligence, especially deep learning techniques like machine optimization, automated processing of LiDAR 3D point datasets has become more efficient. This can lead to improved outcomes at reasonable computational costs. The machine intelligence LiDAR 3D point datasets tool is a free, open-source program written in Python that allows users to automatically process and refine LiDAR 3D point datasets based on input parameters. It can also be utilized as a module within other projects due to its compatible Python 3 writing style.

This work is associated with examining a specific type of random matrix, specifically an $N\times M$ matrix $\mathbf{X}$ composed of real numbers, where the matrix elements are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) following a specific probability distribution. When this matrix is normalized by a factor of $\sqrt{N}$, the resulting matrix can be represented as a random field on the unit sphere in $N$ dimensions with stochastic parameters $N$ and $M$. This connection between the normalized matrix and the unit sphere is useful for calculating the recursive relationships for static random matrices of the Chebyshev-Gibbs type. It also allows for the development of similar recursive relationships for their corresponding random fields on the unit sphere.

The Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina has the capability to pinpoint the origins and energies of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and has identified three intriguing cases of neutrinos whose directions align with these UHECRs within a 10-degree angular range. Due to the low statistical significance of this correlation, a theoretical model was created to assess the likelihood of such correlations occurring randomly. This model took into account the effects of neutrino clustering near Earth and the observation biases of the Pierre Auger Observatory, resulting in maximum probabilities of less than one percent. Consequently, there is a limited, yet non-negligible, chance of a local spatial relationship between the sources of neutrinos and UHECRs, which could have important cosmic implications. To strengthen this relationship, a more sensitive analyzer is being utilized, while expanding the observational data set is also expected to provide a more thorough examination.

We find that liquid foams display a unique frictional property stemming from their textured surface. Our research reveals that the friction between two parallel foam layers varies directly with the tension between them, and that this friction reaches a point where it exceeds the tension ratio at which the foam begins to behave like a turbulent mixture. This ratio is found to be around 0.08, observed in volatile non-adherent foams made from small particles. This surface tension ratio is likely an important factor in the development of turbulent mixtures and should be considered in studies of turbulent flows involving turbulent bubbly flows. This phenomenon should also be present in systems featuring large-scale turbulent mixtures.

This report focuses on creating a method to categorize various types of skin tumors, including benign, malignant, and normal skin, using advanced deep learning technology. We utilize the dermis.net database and employ the Net classifier to analyze images. To accurately distinguish between normal, benign, and malignant skin, we manipulate the network's capacity and combine it with a decision support system based on entropy. Our approach enables us to identify and separate cases of atypical skin from images that are clearly normal, benign, or malignant skin.

A polymer solution is examined in a vertical, rotating Hele-Shaw cell, where it is dispensed onto a gap-surface and subjected to centrifugal forces causing it to spread out. The fluid's edge forms a distinctive barrier known as a contact line. When the cell's rotation rate surpasses a specific threshold, the contact line develops a rotation-induced instability, prompting "fingers" of polymer to spin out from the main body. These fingers can be induced to form at will by manipulating the cell's rotation speed and the polymer concentration. Observing the system through a microscope in the cell's frame of reference, researchers found that the fingers can be seen moving back and forth as they oscillate in sync with the cell's rotation. A series of hysteresis curves generated from varying the system's parameters, along with accompanying polymer traces, help define the flexible nature of the polymer fingers in this unique setup.

Voltaire once remarked, "For all evil originates from bad design," a sentiment we feel can be substituted with design flaws resulting from time constraints. One such limitation arises from the phase space variation that influences simulation speed in molecular dynamics simulations. Typically, the more complex a system is, with more particles and stronger interactions, control over its behavior can be easily compromised, even with ample time. We propose a novel approach, designed to overcome this restriction, allows for molecular dynamics simulations to be completed in the same amount of time, whether for a system with thousands of particles with complex interactions or for a single particle with no interactions. We now can, for instance, simulate the expansion of millions of particles with no external influences, with the same degree of accuracy and precision as a single particle, simply by increasing the simulation time step.

A recent analysis predicts the presence of TMC-1's ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5-CCH) at a velocity V(L11)=-8.6km/s, a specific signal identified through a self-consistent analysis of 3mm and 1.3mm data. Attention mechanisms have seen significant success in various tasks, including neural machine translation. However, existing approaches only consider past and current information due to efficiency concerns. To address this limitation, this research proposes ULTRA, a bidirectional attention mechanism that also incorporates future information. As ULTRA's look-forward depth increases, it effectively integrates more target information while maintaining computational effectiveness. Our experiments show that ULTRA consistently outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin, with notable improvements particularly evident in longer translation outputs. Furthermore, ULTRA outperforms a highly effective baseline by a significant margin, proving its production readiness. Our model codes are available on GitHub for reference.

This informal talk is not about a translational theory or framework in the context of computer science. Instead, it aims to clarify the use of the term 'translational' within our project at the University of Colorado, which involves creating a grid for the translation of petabytes of neutrino data into a format that can be visualized and analyzed by researchers. We will explain our grid translation framework, which is designed to handle and process this vast amount of data, and discuss its significance in the development of our project.

A novel framework known as 'Combined Dark Fluid' has emerged, which posits that mysterious dark matter and dark energy can be unified into a single entity with unknown physical properties. This model suggests that this combined substance possesses both matter-like and energy-like behavior, yet it is gradually losing its internal energy due to dissipation. The framework has since been developed within the context of an expanding universe following the Big Bang theory. Theoretical calculations were then conducted using relativistic fluid dynamics to determine the model's dissipation characteristics. The resulting findings suggest that the model exhibits rotational spinning behavior, a gradual flattening of the universe, and, importantly, that it successfully avoids the pathologies associated with the Big Rip scenario.

Curiosity is a vital human trait that fuels vital learning and driving forces for essential problem-solving, yet its nature remains relatively unexplored.  To better understand curiosity's complexity, we need systematic methods to observe and study it in real-world social learning situations.  By utilizing a newly developed approach that combines social network analysis with machine learning, we can investigate how the way people interact during group learning opportunities can indicate their level of curiosity.  When presented with ambiguous problems during problem-solving learning, inquisitive individuals often ask for help and seek out new information to bridge knowledge gaps.  By analyzing patterns of information flow among group members, we can create a measurable indicator of curiosity within the learning group.  Our research discovered that this method is a powerful predictor of overall learning improvement and can be reliably measured through both self-assessments and actual performance.  Additionally, our analysis discovered that curiosity is not a uniform state of knowledge, but rather composed of multiple, distinct aspects that respond to stimulation in unique ways.  Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for further exploration of curiosity's role in learning and suggests that analyzing information flow may provide a new lens through which to view this fascinating phenomenon.

Spatial statistical analysis in three-dimensional space is commonly based on the Mat\'ern covariance model, which has simple and maintainable characteristics for analysis. However, the application of this model is limited to small-scale projects due to the high computational costs of certain operations. Researchers have developed alternative methods that leverage fast solvers to overcome this drawback, particularly in Cartesian coordinate systems. In a recent study, we propose an adaptation of the Mat\'ern model suitable for analyzing spatial data associated with irregular graphs, which represents a larger and more complex dataset than regularly spaced points. Although there are some theoretical limitations to this model, we demonstrate that it provides an appropriate approximation for a wide range of real-world datasets. Specifically, we show that it can accurately model the spectral properties of various graphs, which we verify through regression tests using actual data. As a result, this model offers a reliable tool for regularized regression, which has been confirmed by its performance in multiple practical scenarios, even when the graph has a high level of complexity.

The effectiveness of a well-managed transportation system relies heavily on the ability to monitor and manage current traffic conditions. Observing the movements of a large number of mobile entities within the city, such as ridesharing vehicles, provides real-time information about the urban road network. This paper aims to develop a method for monitoring traffic and mapping the network of streets by utilizing data from these vehicles. The proposed method offers various ways to observe different aspects of the road network, including its overall capacity, by analyzing the movements of these agents within a clearly defined network. A case study using real-world data tests the effectiveness of the developed method and highlights its ability to provide insights into the street network.

The decay of $J/\psi$ into visible and invisible particles has been studied for a long time. Recent advancements in laboratory and astronomical research in the areas of neutrinos and dark energy have led to the development of effective field theories, specifically Neutrino Effective Field Theory (nEFT) and Low-Energy Effective Field Theory (LEET). Within these frameworks, precise predictions about theJ/\psi decay into invisible particles can be made. The new global analysis combines world-wide data on neutrino oscillations, mixing angles and other parameters to make significant insights about the J/\psi decay, yielding a standard model value of $\Gamma^{(\gamma + {\rm inv})}_{J/\psi}/\Gamma_{J/\psi}=0.00848\pm0.00016$ and a confidence interval of $[0.00658, 0.01038]$. Furthermore, the analysis establishes constraints on the coefficients of the LEET, with the most stringent limits being set on the coefficients linked to the $J/\psi$ decay, yielding a standard model consistent range of $-0.24\le0/d_{\pi}^3\le0.24\, {\rm fm}^3$.
